Thanks, I confirm that multithreading now beats multiprocessing: Here's the flame graph I get now: Good: we're now spending more time inside the `sin` and `cos` implementations, which is where we want to be. Bad: There's some contention to acquire a critical section in `convert_ufunc_arguments`, ultimately called by the `array_add` implementation. Because this is all in NumPy internals I wonder if there's a way we can know statically that there's no mutation going on and the critical section is unnecessary. But maybe it is necessary? Or maybe we should not worry so much about people trying to break NumPy by mutating the argument of `np.array()` while an array is being created in another thread. There's also a bit of contention in the `shared_mutex` in the promotion cache. Maybe @kumaraditya303 PyMutex-based RWLock will perform better (see https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/30275). Also see [the full profile](https://share.firefox.dev/45kngQE) for more detail.

For the array coercion critical section: one thing we can do right now is skip it when immutable data are passed in. So we could check for lists vs tuples, for example. We can also maybe check the readonly flag?

For the `shared_mutex` i'm increasingly thinking we should bite the bullet and implement the suggestion in https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/30275#issuecomment-3572007197. The `shared_mutex` I get from the Apple Clang LibC++ seems to hit a slow path - even for shared reads with no writes (as fast as I can see, maybe I'm missing something).

if I only (i) **read** the data that threads can see, and (ii) **create** new numpy arrays in each thread during parallelization, and (iii) allow no thread communication before the final join, will the bottleneck _mostly_ depend on the concurrent efficiency of low-level allocators like `malloc`? And I say _mostly_ because i'm sure great (compared to C-level) overhead exists in the Python layer so we shouldn't let threads create many small numpy arrays or work on trivial tasks.

```
import numpy as np
import os
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor

# `x` is referenced `n_loop` times.
def kernel(x, n_loop):
    return sum((np.sin(np.cos(np.sin(np.cos(x + i)))).sum() 
        for i in range(n_loop)))

def worker(group, n_loop):
    return sum(kernel(g, n_loop) for g in group)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    import sys
    print("Python version is free-threaded:", not sys._is_gil_enabled())
    vsize = 500
    n = 100000
    np.random.seed(42)

    X = [np.random.uniform(size = vsize) for _ in range(n)]
    n_core = os.cpu_count()
    dx = len(X) // n_core + 1
    Xgroups = []
    for i in range(0, len(X), dx):
        Xgroups.append(X[i:min(i+dx, len(X))])

    import time, mtmp

    n_loop = 50

    st = time.time()
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers = n_core) as pool:
        futures = [pool.submit(mtmp.worker, g, n_loop) for g in Xgroups]
        workerRsts = [future.result() for future in futures]
    print(f"Inner loops {n_loop}, multiprocessing time: { \
        time.time() - st:.2f} sec, result sum: {sum(workerRsts)}")

    st = time.time()
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers = n_core) as pool:
        futures = [pool.submit(mtmp.worker, g, n_loop) for g in Xgroups]
        workerRsts = [future.result() for future in futures]
    print(f"Inner loops {n_loop}, multithreading  time: { \
        time.time() - st:.2f} sec, result sum: {sum(workerRsts)}")

```

I still see some multithreaded scaling issues here due to global state in NumPy. See this profile: https://share.firefox.dev/3YLcFuu.

I think the problem is that even though NumPy's allocator is stored in a context variable, that doesn't mean that the handler is automatically thread-local. Instead, I think because the allocator context variable just uses `PyDataMem_DefaultHandler` as the default value, that means that each worker by default uses the global allocator and that leads to contention. Both refcount contention and also heap contention inside `malloc`.

See here: https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/e017416123fe471c9a3f9a36bcb98223fd7cba1d/numpy/_core/src/multiarray/multiarraymodule.c#L5180. The second argument to `PyContextVar_New` is the default value.

Instead, we probably want a per-thread PyCapsule pointer to the allocator? That'll help the refcount contention.

For the `malloc` contention, it'll probably help to turn on the allocator cache for all these small allocations in your script, see #30499.

I created a branch with all of the WIP optimizations we're working on as well as @colesbury's suggestion to make the memory handler immortal. I also noticed a similar reference counting contention issue with the floating point exception handler PyCapsule and made that immortal as well. You can pull the [`fast-cache` branch](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/compare/main...ngoldbaum:numpy:fast-cache?expand=1) from my fork of NumPy to get the code.

With that code and [this script](https://gist.github.com/ngoldbaum/b01b00365498acc73e27eba4c1dfc401) which sets `n_workers` and `n_loop` to 50, I get the following profile: https://share.firefox.dev/3L48gjb. On my Mac developer machine, multithreading beats multiprocessing by a 10% margin.

I also ran the script using jemalloc, which does seem to help a little but it doesn't fix the malloc contention I see in the profile. The allocator cache is turned on but it doesn't seem like it helps much. Maybe there's more we can do to improve allocation caching so there are fewer cache misses?

I also see a small scaling issue in `_Py_module_getattro_impl `. I also see an opportunity to maybe get a tiny performance boost by bypassing the `name_matches` check inside the `PyCapsule_GetPointer` implementation. Maybe there's room for a variant that doesn't check the capsule name?

After that, I don't see any more obvious multithreaded bottlenecks. Everything else looks like code from the core ufunc loop, reductions, or scalar math.

This behaviour is well-known. See the notes section [here](https://numpy.org/devdocs/reference/generated/numpy.sum.html). The rule of thumb is to always accumulate in float64, even if your source data is float32, i.e.,

```
s1 = np.sum(tmp[:, 1], dtype=np.float64)
s2 = np.sum(tmp, axis=0, dtype=np.float64)[1]
```

I was able to reproduce this on Windows with OpenBLAS.

This appears to be expected floating-point behavior due to different reduction paths and accumulation order.

Observations:
- `np.sum(arr[:, i])` uses a 1-D reduction path, while `np.sum(arr, axis=0)` uses a vectorized/parallel reduction (OpenBLAS).
- With `float32`, non-associativity causes different rounding errors.
- Using `dtype=np.float64` for accumulation yields the exact result.
- Forcing single-threaded OpenBLAS (`OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1`) significantly reduces the discrepancy.

This seems consistent with the NumPy documentation recommending float64 accumulation for large reductions.

Oh, and for errors, I think the logic we want is:

import numbers
def sqrt_fallback(obj):
    if hasattr(obj, "sqrt"):
        # Any exception here is allowed to escape:
        return obj.sqrt()
    transformed_obj = None
    mod = None
    try:
        transformed_obj = float(obj)
        mod = math
    except TypeError:
        try:
            transformed_obj = complex(obj)
            mod = cmath
        except TypeError:
            raise TypeError("object has no .sqrt() method, and isn't
convertible to float or complex")
    # Any exception here is allowed to escape
    return mod.sqrt(transformed_obj)

(We may well want to literally implement the whole fallback lookup logic in

the function name as a parameter instead of copying all that code above for
all the different ufuncs, like ufunc_obj_fallback(ufunc_name, obj). And
then the C level code could just call this Python function unconditionally.)

So proposing one more idea: Every `dot` input case can be delegate to some ufunc

| Case | Dispatch to |
|---|---|
| either is 0-D | `multiply` (already done in current C) |
| 1-D × 1-D | `vecdot` |
| ≥2-D × 1-D | `matvec` |
| 1-D × ≥2-D | `vecmat` |
| 2-D × 2-D | `matmul` |
| N-D × M-D | reshape to 2D → `matmul` → reshape back (the tensordot trick) |

For performance, this should be equal or better than today. The current `N-D × M-D` C path runs a nested iterator loop calling a 1D `dotfunc` per output element, but `tensordot` already does this better, reshapes both inputs to 2D, calls `dot`, and reshapes back. We'd just close the loop by having `dot` call `matmul` instead, so the chain becomes `tensordot -> dot -> matmul` with everything going through ufunc dispatch.

This alone would fix `dot`, `inner` (transposes then calls `dot`), `tensordot` (reshapes then calls `dot`), and `multi_dot` (calls `dot`) -- all without any user-visible behavior change. `vdot` needs a small separate fix (conjugate + flatten + `vecdot`).

The root cause of all the user-dtype breakage is `PyArray_ObjectType`, which rejects non-legacy dtypes. By dispatching to ufuncs  we sidestep this entirely.

I also think this could just live at the Python level (similar to how `tensordot` is already implemented in Python), keeping the C path as a fast path for legacy dtypes if we want to be conservative about performance changes.

Hi. We were checking differences between v1 and v2 for migration, are found some more examples:

```python
# v1.26.4
>>> np.where(np.array([[0, 1]], dtype=np.uint8), 1000, 0)
>>> np.where(np.array([[0, 1]], dtype=np.uint8), 1000, np.uint8(0))
array([[   0, 1000]]) # dtype=int64
>>> np.where(np.array([[0, 1]], dtype=np.uint8), 1000, np.array([[50, 0]], dtype=np.uint8))
array([[  50, 1000]], dtype=uint16)

# v2.2.6
# using simply y = 0 and x = 1000 silently upcasts the condition type
>>> np.where(np.array([[0, 1]], dtype=np.uint8), 1000, 0)
array([[   0, 1000]]) # dtype=int64

# casting y to uint8 array silently downcasts x and truncates it
>>> np.where(np.array([[0, 1]], dtype=np.uint8), 1000, np.uint8(0))
array([[  0, 232]], dtype=uint8)
>>> np.where(np.array([[0, 1]], dtype=np.uint8), 1000, np.array([[50, 0]], dtype=np.uint8))
array([[50, 76]], dtype=uint8)
```
The result that we get in v1 (uint16) is the desired outcome, at least, for us. If there's a silent upcasting to int64 happens, there are also possible hidden issues that the resulting array occupies more memory that it could - basically, `sizeof(int64) / sizeof(uint16)`, and requires more compute for processing (e.g. in the case of vectorized loops). Silent truncation is not expected.

The workaround we found (likely, it's the intended implementation now) - cast x and y to the desired type:
```python
# v2.2.6
# casting x = 1000 to min dtype array works fine
>>> np.where(np.array([[0, 1]], dtype=np.uint8), np.array(1000, np.min_scalar_type(1000)), 0)
array([[   0, 1000]], dtype=uint16)
>>> np.where(np.array([[0, 1]], dtype=np.uint8), np.array(1000, np.min_scalar_type(1000)), np.array([[50, 0]], dtype=np.uint8))
array([[  50, 1000]], dtype=uint16)
```

We couldn't find how this behavior could be justified by the broadcasting rules, but if the condition dtype is not considered, it makes more sense. I think it would be useful to mention this in the documentation somehow, if the behavior is intended, and avoid silent casting. There's an error for truncation in v2 in `multiply()`:

While I was just hunting memory leak in my long running trainer process, I ended up finding that it is also slower than my work around! I couldn't build numpy from source yet to test the fix. So, if anyone is going to test it, I am sharing my test code below.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import sys
import numpy as np
import gc
import time
import psutil
import os
import platform
from typing import Callable

MY_PID = os.getpid()
MY_PROC = psutil.Process(MY_PID)

def get_memory_mb(proc=MY_PROC) -> float:
    """Get current process RSS memory in MB."""
    return proc.memory_info().rss / (1024 * 1024)


def create_test_array(i: int, shape: tuple, dtype=np.uint32) -> np.ndarray:
    """Create test arrays cycling through uniform and mixed patterns."""
    if np.issubdtype(dtype, np.integer):
        patterns = [
            lambda: np.ones(shape, dtype=dtype),           # All 1s
            lambda: np.zeros(shape, dtype=dtype),          # All 0s
            lambda: np.random.randint(0, 2, shape, dtype=dtype)  # Mixed 0s and 1s
        ]
    else:  # float32 or other float types
        patterns = [
            lambda: np.full(shape, 1.0, dtype=dtype),      # All 1.0s
            lambda: np.zeros(shape, dtype=dtype),          # All 0.0s
            lambda: np.random.randn(*shape).astype(dtype)  # Mixed
        ]
    return patterns[i % len(patterns)]()


def benchmark_operation(
    operation: Callable[[np.ndarray], bool],
    num_iterations: int = 10_000,
    array_size: tuple = (512, 512),
    dtype=np.uint32,
    name: str = "Operation"
) -> dict:
    """
    Benchmark a numpy operation and measure memory growth.
    
    Args:
        operation: Function that takes an array and returns bool
        num_iterations: Number of iterations to run
        array_size: Shape of test arrays
        dtype: NumPy dtype for arrays
        name: Name of the operation for reporting
        
    Returns:
        dict with baseline_mb, final_mb, growth_mb, elapsed_sec
    """
    gc.collect()
    time.sleep(0.1)
    baseline_mb = get_memory_mb()
    start_time = time.time()
    
    for i in range(num_iterations):
        arr = create_test_array(i, array_size, dtype)
        _ = operation(arr)
        del arr
    
    gc.collect()
    time.sleep(0.1)
    final_mb = get_memory_mb()
    elapsed = time.time() - start_time
    
    return {
        'name': name,
        'iterations': num_iterations,
        'dtype': dtype.__name__,
        'baseline_mb': baseline_mb,
        'final_mb': final_mb,
        'growth_mb': final_mb - baseline_mb,
        'elapsed_sec': elapsed,
        'avg_leak_kb': (final_mb - baseline_mb) * 1024 / num_iterations if num_iterations > 0 else 0
    }


def print_results(results: dict, show_leak_warning: bool = True):
    """Pretty print benchmark results."""
    print(f"\n{'='*70}")
    print(f"{results['name']} ({results['dtype']})")
    print(f"{'='*70}")
    print(f"Iterations:     {results['iterations']:,}")
    print(f"Elapsed:        {results['elapsed_sec']:.2f} seconds")
    print(f"Baseline:       {results['baseline_mb']:.2f} MB")
    print(f"Final:          {results['final_mb']:.2f} MB")
    print(f"Growth:         {results['growth_mb']:.2f} MB")
    print(f"Leak per call:  {results['avg_leak_kb']:.2f} KB")
    
    if show_leak_warning and results['growth_mb'] > 1:
        print(f"\n⚠️  MEMORY LEAK DETECTED")
    elif results['growth_mb'] < 1:
        print(f"\n✓ No significant memory leak")
    print(f"{'='*70}")


def main():
    """Run benchmarks comparing np.unique() vs min/max workaround."""
    print(f"\nNumPy Memory Leak Reproduction")
    print(f"NumPy version: {np.__version__}")
    print(f"Python version: {'.'.join(map(str, sys.version_info[:3]))} ")
    print(f"Platform : {platform.system()} {platform.release()} ({platform.machine()})\n")
    
    array_size = (512, 512)
    num_iterations = 1_000
    dtypes = [np.uint32, np.float32]
    
    for dtype in dtypes:
        print(f"Testing {dtype.__name__} arrays - Shape: {array_size}, Iterations: {num_iterations:,}")
        
        res_uniq = benchmark_operation(
            operation=lambda arr: len(np.unique(arr)) <= 1,
            num_iterations=num_iterations,
            array_size=array_size,
            dtype=dtype,
            name="np.unique() - Check for single value"
        )
        print_results(res_uniq)
        
        res_minmax = benchmark_operation(
            operation=lambda arr: arr.min() == arr.max(),
            num_iterations=num_iterations,
            array_size=array_size,
            dtype=dtype,
            name="arr.min() == arr.max() - Workaround"
        )
        print_results(res_minmax, show_leak_warning=False)
        
        print()
        speedup = res_uniq['elapsed_sec'] / res_minmax['elapsed_sec']

In most cases that wouldn't be possible I'm afraid. For example when a function is overloaded or if its generic, it isn't possible to document the types of the parameters and output *independently*. So the annotations are often simply too complex to be able to document in the format that we use.

For example, this is what the `np.stack` stubs look like:

https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/0e5814954b418ad591c1fefc969d2e4dfb8c6d2b/numpy/_core/shape_base.pyi#L122-L167

Also note that these overloads for `stack` are relatively simple; there are many significantly more complex functions out there, some with more than 30 overloads.

I actually think it's good that the docs use different notation for describing parameter types, because it's an *informal* description, as opposed to the *formal* type annotations in the stubs.

This is working as expected: when you index with multiple boolean indices, the masks are not applied in sequence, but rather the indices of the `True` elements are broadcast together (see https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.indexing.html#boolean-array-indexing).

So this:
```python
a[[False], [True, True]]
```
would be equivalent to
```python
a[np.nonzero([False]), np.nonzero([True, True])]
```
which is equivalent to
```python
a[[], [0, 1]]
```
as mentioned at https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.indexing.html#integer-array-indexing, when you index with two integer arrays, those indices are broadcast together: `[]` (a sequence of length zero) cannot be broadcast with `[0, 1]` (a sequence of length 2), so you get the error you're seeing.

If you want to apply the indices in sequence rather than broadcasting together, you can do that via two separate indexing operations; e.g.
```python
>>> a[[False]][:, [True, True]]
array([], shape=(0, 2), dtype=float64)
```

@jakevdp @seberg I understand that this do makes sense in terms of converting-to-nonzero-sense. But in terms of the philosophy of "fancy index broadcasts together", this convert-to-nonzero-then-broadcast is kind of opposite to directly broadcast, which feel wired:

When we do `np.empty((2,2))[np.ones(2,'?'),np.ones(2,'?')]`, that actually means diagonal instead of full matrix, which "suggests" that boolean masks are not auto "raised" to corresponding dimension, they're directly broadcasted.

Then when we do `np.empty((2,2))[np.ones((2,1),'?'),np.ones(2,'?')]` (i.e. manually raising), this becomes an Exception. Since now we're indexing 2d array with 3d index, which "suggests" that boolean masks are do raised, since the first mask is raised by one dimension.

When we do `np.empty((2,2))[np.ones((2,1),'?')&np.ones(2,'?')]` (i.e. manually broadcasting), now it works as intended meshgrid, but now we're materializing a large boolean matrix, which would be disastrous if both mask is sparse.

When we apply mask manually twice, firstly this creates temporary copy, secondly setitem would not work.

When we use things like np.ix_ or np.nonzero, essentially we're converting mask to index, which I feel (not verified) should be less efficient, especially when there's a lot of true in the mask, and as a result we're generating an 8x (bool->long) larger temporary array than the mask? Letting the numpy core handle this conversion implicitly might leverage some kind of internal chunk/fused optimization?

As a result, we can never(?) implement an efficient and fully functional multiple-boolean-mask-product indexing?

Multiple boolean indices cannot broadcast directly because this is incompatible with the semantics of single boolean indices, which is to consume the number of dimensions of the boolean array. This differs from indexing with integer arrays, where a single dimension is consumed regardless of the dimension of the index array.

If you want broadcasting semantics without explicit computation of the broadcasted mask, I think `x[np.nonzero(i1)[:, None], np.nonzero(i2)]` is probably your best option.

Fixing this would likely require either:

* writing in place then undoing (not thread-safe)
* Adding a `where` argument to `ufunc.reduce` (hard!)

Just in case someone wonders why adding `where` is hard: these masks for normal ufunc use are not actually seen by the internal loops: rather they just do whatever is needed on chunks of data, producing a chunk of output; `where` only is used to tell whether to copy a given bit of the latter to the actual output array. Since for the reduce operations, the addition is done in-place in the output chunk, it is too late to do masking.

It is also one of many places where it would be wonderful to be able to "chain" ufuncs, in which the chain does not operate on the whole array, but by chunk.

The Intel compilers trigger a segmentation fault inside one of their optimization passes. As far as my testing goes, this affects oneAPI 2025.2.1 and 2025.2.0, but not oneAPI 2025.1.1. There seems to be some kind of regression.
I've already created a bug report for this (Bug ID 06682863). Hopefully this can be fixed, or a workaround can be found.

Testing of different platforms shows that this doesn't occur with all architectures though. Alder Lake with `-march=native` and Zen 5 `-march=core-avx2` failed, but Genoa worked with `-march=rocketlake`.

Workaround that builds and passes test suite:

In https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/main/numpy/_core/meson.build#L937 edit line 937 to remove `AVX512_SKX, AVX512F, AVX2, `. This avoids building the AVX2 version of `loops_arithmetic` and that is what is being built when the compiler segfaults.

I've been able to compile numpy 2.3.2 on top of python 3.11.11 using intel oneapi compilers 2024.2.1 with an explicit `-march=skylake-avx512` flag. It detected all the available AVX* options. Given how fragile this build process is, I'll just let sleeping dogs lie and make this our new setup. I do have some `numpy.test()` failures, but I'll open a separate ticket for that.

1) Python 3.10 has deprecated the distutils module for building Python C extensions. So, newer versions of setuptools (which follow the new protocol) error out when the disutils module is used to build anything (which NumPy does). So, building NumPy with any setuptools > v60.0.0 doesn't work. You will have to downgrade setuptools to any version < 60.0.0.

Do the above then try to run tests.

2)  check if you are `building from source` and then running the tests. If perhaps you are installing numpy via `pip install numpy` then there could be a version mishap. To clarify, it is correct to not explicitly add `/usr/include` to _all_ compiler invocations because it breaks cross-compilation.

However, `/usr/include` is in the default search path:
```
$ echo | gcc -E -Wp,-v -
ignoring nonexistent directory "/usr/lib/gcc/x86_64-redhat-linux/11/include-fixed"
ignoring nonexistent directory "/usr/lib/gcc/x86_64-redhat-linux/11/../../../../x86_64-redhat-linux/include"
#include "..." search starts here:
#include <...> search starts here:
 /usr/lib/gcc/x86_64-redhat-linux/11/include
 /usr/local/include
 /usr/include
End of search list.
# 0 "<stdin>"
# 0 "<built-in>"
# 0 "<command-line>"
# 1 "/usr/include/stdc-predef.h" 1 3 4
# 0 "<command-line>" 2
# 1 "<stdin>"

$ cat foo.c 
#include <fftw3.h>

$ gcc -c foo.c 
# No error finding the header.
```

So however `system_info` is searching for headers, it is _ignoring_ default include paths.

> So however `system_info` is searching for headers, it is _ignoring_ default include paths.

Yes indeed. Unfortunately, it's just a bunch of hardcoded paths: https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/main/numpy/distutils/system_info.py#L326

Given that `numpy.distutils` is deprecated and it has been like this for 15 years, I don't really want to spend time on fixing things up. What I suggest is you simply add back `/usr/include` in your `setup.py` file via:
```python
from numpy.distutils import system_info
from numpy.distutils import system_info.append('/usr/include')
```

I got bitten by this. It's not in the documentation for [np.divide](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/numpy/reference/generated/numpy.divide.html#numpy.divide) at all. I eventually found this bug report which references the [ufuncs](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/numpy/reference/ufuncs.html#ufuncs-kwargs) documentation. I had looked at those, but I was mostly reading the `where` part, and not the `out` part, since I thought I already understood what that did by reading about it in the `np.divide` documentation.

The [current documentation for `where`](http://www.numpy.org/devdocs/reference/generated/numpy.divide.html) states "values of False indicate to leave the value in the output alone". What would you suggest as an alternative?

My (naive) interpretation of "leave the value in the output alone" was that the those values would remain what they were in `x1` rather than the current default which is an uninitialized array. My inclination is to either
- adopt @bersbersbers' option 1 in [their original post](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/11417#issue-335352450):
 > Require an `out` parameter when a `where` parameter is used. Make people who avoid divisions by zero add `out=None`, just to make sure everyone knows they are using non-initialized output and are OK with that. Don't assume anything from the non-presence of `out`.
- or change the documentation to say:
> values of False indicate to leave the value in the output alone. Note that these values are uninitialized unless `out` is explicitly specified.

If my incident yesterday is at all representative of others who've been stumped by this, the following [ufuncs documentation](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/numpy/reference/ufuncs.html#ufuncs-kwargs) was what finally resolved the issue for me.

> If `out` is None (the default), a uninitialized return array is created. The output array is then filled with the results of the ufunc in the places that the broadcast `where` is True. If `where` is the scalar True (the default), then this corresponds to the entire output being filled. Note that outputs not explicitly filled are left with their uninitialized values.
Closing, we now warn if `where` is used without `out`.

There are some technical limitations (C code has to go in C files, etc.), and if the API you're adding will be exposed through a public submodule like `np.linalg` or `np.ma` then obviously you should take that into account, but otherwise I don't think there is any consistent rule. The layout has always struck me as somewhat idiosyncratic, probably reflecting some off-the-cuff choices in the early days, and then I think since then people have just used the rule of "think of what the most similar existing function is, and put my function next to it".

It should be noted that in general the `where` will be overshadowed by the `is it necessary`, any new unique functionality (not simply adding `quantile` to `percentile to take a recent example) will need to be discussed on the mailing list and you will need to convince people that it belongs in NumPy rather than SciPy.

Creating a dtype for complex integers is feasible, but is it worthwhile?  Questions for anyone looking for this: what are you going to *do* with your array of complex integers?  What operations do you want to perform?  Basic arithmetic would not be difficult, but many of the mathematical functions implemented in NumPy and SciPy expect floating point inputs, so if you try to use them, your data will eventually be cast to floating point.  For example, I'm pretty sure there is no implementation of the FFT in NumPy or SciPy that is specifically for integers, so if you want to compute the FFT of your complex integer array, you'll have to convert to one of the complex floating point representations.

@WarrenWeckesser  I think your intuition is correct that there would be limitations to a `complex_int_NN` type, but this is not unique to complex integers.  This is a general problem when dealing with fixed bitwidth integers. You get weird answers if you don't convert your data to a type that can handle the operation.  consider
```
>>> np.square( np.int16( [ 181, 182 ] ) )
array([ 32761, -32412], dtype=int16)
```

### Motivation for complex integers
The use case for complex integers is anywhere large amounts of complex data are to be stored efficiently.  One might want to analyze/modify slices of the data (e.g. via memmapped file) without converting the whole thing.
Here are some example applications 
* radio signals digitized in "complex baseband" format
* MRI raw samples
* synthetic aperture radar (SAR) raw data
* seismic data
* Fourier data of any kind

As python (and jupyter) grows more popular for dealing with huge datasets, so does the need for a workable complex integer type.

### Desired behavior
What would be nice is if basic manipulation worked as expected *or* gave an error when trying to do so. 
```
# a complex `view` of integer data, analogous to casting  float32 as complex64
civec = some_ndarray_of_int16.view(  np.complex_int_32 )

# setting from a complex value should behave as expected
civec[:] = 1+2j # broadcasts/interleave int16 1,2 

# setting from a real value should zero the imag part, and vice versa
civec[:] = 42

# get/set  real or imag parts through attributes/properties
q = civec[:].imag # q should be an array of np.int16
civec[:].imag *= -1   # creates the complex conjugate  (same as q *= -1) 

# math manipulations should either work as expected or fail loudly
# (the former is more tempting, but perilous)
d = civec + civec # what is "expected" here?  wrap? clip?  promote sometimes? always?

# convert to a complex floating point class when more math is required
F = np.fft.fft( civec.astype(np.complex64) )
```

### Partial solutions
Note a user-customized dtype (e.g. `np.dtype([('real', np.int16), ('imag', np.int16)])` )
is not even close to the above desired behavior.

The main difference between `numpy.char.rjust` and `str.rjust` is in the input they accept and the output they return.

`numpy.char.rjust` is a NumPy function that operates on arrays of strings. It accepts an array-like object (a) containing strings and right-justifies each element of the array in a string of length width. The resulting output is an `ndarray` containing the right-justified strings.

On the other hand, `str.rjust` is a method available for individual string objects in Python. It right-justifies a single string (s) within a string of length width and returns the resulting right-justified string.

                import numpy as np
                
                # Using numpy.char.rjust
                arr = np.array(['apple', 'banana', 'cherry'])
                result = np.char.rjust(arr, 8)
                print(result)
                # Output: ['   apple' '  banana' '  cherry']
                
                # Using str.rjust
                s = 'hello'
                result = s.rjust(10)
                print(result)
                # Output: '     hello'


So, the key differences lie in the input type (array-like vs. individual string) and the output type (ndarray vs. single string).

The main difference between `numpy.char.rjust` and `str.rjust` is in how they handle strings that are longer than the specified width.

`numpy.char.rjust` behaves differently from `str.rjust` when it comes to strings that are longer than the specified width. According to the current implementation of numpy.char.rjust, if a string's length exceeds the specified width, it will be truncated to fit within that width. This means that characters from the end of the string will be removed to match the specified width.

On the other hand, `str.rjust` returns the original string unchanged if its length is greater than or equal to the specified width. It does not truncate or modify the original string.

            import numpy as np

Therefore, it is important to note that the behavior of `numpy.char.rjust` differs from the behavior of `str.rjust`, especially when dealing with strings that are longer than the specified width. The documentation for `numpy.char.rjust` should reflect this behavior to avoid confusion.

The problem has nothing to do with SciPy's sparse matrices.  The problem is apparently a bug (or perhaps just a "gotcha") in how `np.roll` handles `matrix` arguments when `axis=None`.  `Y[0].todense()` returns a `matrix` (not `ndarray`) with shape (1, 5), and applying `roll` to this matrix exposes the unexpected behavior.

For example, in the following, `np.roll(a, 1)` works as expected:
```
In [74]: a = np.array([[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]])

In [75]: np.roll(a, 1)
Out[75]: array([[4, 0, 1, 2, 3]])
```
Given that, it is surprising that `np.roll(m, 1)` does not produce a similar result in the following:
```
In [76]: m = np.matrix([[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]])

In [77]: np.roll(m, 1)
Out[77]: matrix([[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]])
```
The docstring for `roll` says that if `axis=None` (the default), "the array is flattened before shifting, after which the original shape is restored", and here's what `roll` returns when `axis` is None:
https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/887766071724d27431b453b8270f299213b2d189/numpy/core/numeric.py#L1213

The problem is that the `ravel()` method does not flatten a `matrix`.  `matrix` objects can't really be "flattened"--at least not while remaining `matrix` objects.  They insist on remaining 2-d:
```
In [78]: m.ravel()
Out[78]: matrix([[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]])

In [79]: m.flatten()
Out[79]: matrix([[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]])
```
so `np.roll(m, 1)` ends up rolling the 2-d matrix along axis 0, which has length 1, so there is no effect.

In this example, a workaround is to use `axis=1`:
```
In [80]: np.roll(m, 1, axis=1)
Out[80]: matrix([[4, 0, 1, 2, 3]])
```
Alternatively, avoid the `matrix` class altogether by using the `toarray()` method of SciPy's sparse matrix instead of the `todense()` method:
```
In [87]: y_0 = Y[0].toarray()  # Use `.toarray()` instead of `.todense()`.

In [88]: y_0
Out[88]: array([[1, 0, 0, 0, 0]])

In [89]: np.roll(y_0, 1)
Out[89]: array([[0, 1, 0, 0, 0]]
```

The `matrix` class is destined for deprecation, so it might not be worthwhile spending more time on this quirk.
Eventually scipy will deprecate `todense`. See scipy/scipy#14494

> ## Alternatives Considered
> 
> 1. **Do nothing** - Force every AI library to add `.float()` calls (current state, not scalable)
> 2. **Warn and convert** - numpy accepts bf16, warns, converts to float32 automatically
> 3. **Full support** - Native bf16 dtype with arithmetic operations
> 
> Option 2 would solve 90% of the pain with minimal implementation effort.

Seems to me like Option 2 would be the way to go if that tradeoff were the case. However, the implementation isn't ours to do. The `TypeError: Got unsupported ScalarType BFloat16` is from [`pytorch`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/511d3316abc6a2d632bb25885646d2e6275f8777/torch/csrc/utils/tensor_numpy.cpp#L315). It's their `.numpy()` method. If we implement a `bfloat16` dtype in numpy, `pytorch`'s updated `.numpy()` method would create `bfloat16` numpy arrays and return those. We would never get the chance to "warn and convert to float32 automatically". `pytorch`, on the other hand, could special-case `BFloat16` earlier and do the internal equivalent of `.float().cpu()`, with a warning, before passing it along to the conversion to `ndarray`s.

`pytorch` could also adopt the 3rd party `bfloat16` implementation linked above either as a dependency or vendor it in. I'd like to hear from them. I think this request is more about PyTorch than us, at this point. Now, if they say that they have reasons such that they only support it if it were a builtin numpy dtype, that'd be another thing. Final follow-up and solution:

I can confirm this is not a NumPy regression. The build failure only occurs when using Intel *classic* compilers (icc/icpc/ifort). The errors originate from NumPy’s Google Highway–based SIMD code introduced in NumPy >= 2.0, which Intel classic compilers do not fully support.

Confirmed behavior:
- ❌ Build fails with icc/icpc (classic)
- ✅ Build succeeds with Intel oneAPI compilers (icx/icpx/ifx)
- Same Python (3.11.3), NumPy (2.4.1), and MKL configuration

Solution:
Use Intel oneAPI compilers instead of Intel classic compilers.

Example working build command:

source /opt/intel/oneapi/setvars.sh

CC=icx CXX=icpx FC=ifx
CFLAGS='-fp-model=strict -xCORE-AVX2'
CXXFLAGS='-fp-model=strict -xCORE-AVX2'
FFLAGS='-fp-model=strict -xCORE-AVX2'
python -m pip install . --no-build-isolation -v


Conclusion:
Intel classic compilers are unsupported for NumPy 2.x. Using icx/icpx (or GCC/Clang) is the correct and supported solution. It may be helpful to document this explicitly to avoid confusion for users still relying on icc/icpc.

Since `pocketfft` has a more complex internal decision tree (e.g. so it can use Bluestein's algorithm for near-prime sizes), it also requires more complex memory management and control flow. This is of course complete overkill for transform of lengths below, say, 20. Having persistent plans (like FFTW does) can help a lot here, but also adds much complexity.

That said, there are a few low-hanging fruit: the `malloc/free` in `pass_all`, `rfftp_forward` and `rfftp_backward` could be avoided for small sizes by using a fixed-size local array. But skipping the memory allocation for the twiddle factors for tiny sizes is already way more complicated.

Hi there! I recently noticed a dramatic drop in FFT and convolution performance when using NumPy, and after learning about the migration to pocketfft, realized it's the culprit. Since the above example appears to use small arrays, I thought I'd share another benchmark that illustrates this with larger arrays. The benchmark is below:
```
import sys
from timeit import default_timer
import numpy.fft

fpl = getattr(numpy.fft, 'fftpack_lite', None)
pfi = getattr(numpy.fft, '_pocketfft_internal', None)
pfi = getattr(numpy.fft, 'pocketfft_internal', pfi)

def run_benchmark(f, x, n):
	x_backup = +x
	y = None
	t = default_timer()
	for i in range(n):
		y = f(x)
	dur = default_timer() - t
	assert numpy.array_equal(x, x_backup), "array should not have been mutated"
	assert numpy.allclose(numpy.fft.rfft(x), y)
	return dur

def benchmark_forward_fft(shape, iterations):
	x = numpy.random.random(shape)
	m = 1 << int(len(x)).bit_length()
	x = numpy.pad(x, [(0, m - len(x))], mode='constant', constant_values=0.0)
	if fpl is not None:
		t = run_benchmark(lambda x, plan=fpl.rffti(m): fpl.rfftf(x, plan), x, iterations)
		print("%s: fftpack_lite.rfft: %.2f us/iteration" % (numpy.__version__, t * 1.0E6 / iterations,))
	if pfi is not None:
		t = run_benchmark(lambda x: pfi.execute(x, True, True, 1), x, iterations)
		print("%s: pocketfft.execute: %.2f us/iteration" % (numpy.__version__, t * 1.0E6 / iterations,))

def main(program, shape = 100, iterations = 1 << 18):
	return benchmark_forward_fft(int(shape), int(iterations))

if __name__ == '__main__':
	import sys
	raise SystemExit(main(*sys.argv) or 0)
```

I do not think that this kind of benchmark is helpful in determining the actual speed of the FFT implementation. Calling into a compiled function from Python for a single FFT of length 100 means that most of the time will not be spent computing the transform but rather checking function arguments, preparing data for the call into C etc. 

To demonstrate this, consider:
```
a=np.zeros((1000,100))
%timeit  np.fft.rfft(a,axis=1)
```
This performs 1000 FFTs of length 100 in one go, and on my laptop it takes around 243 microseconds (with pocketfft, I don't have a `numpy` with fftpack installed at the moment). In other words, the real computation time for a single length 100 FFT is a quarter of a microsecond, several times faster than your measured results.

I can imagine two reasons why the `fftpack` version is faster:
- less glue code on the Python side (this has changed a bit in the transition to `pocketfft`). It may be possible to tweak this further, but I'm not sure it's worth the effort
- slower plan generation code in `pocketfft` vs. `fftpack`. This mainly involves computing "twiddle factors", i.e. calling a lot of trigonometric functions. `pocketfft` is emphasizing accuracy here and will probably be slower, while `fftpack` (at least the real-valued FFTs, which you are using) has a pretty bad reputation for accuracy..

I'd argue that if a user requires high performance on small 1D FFTs they should do many of them simultaneously if at all possible. I know that this cannot always be done, but the remaining situations are (in my opinion, and I'm open to counterexamples!) so rare that a general purpose code like `numpy` doesn't need to be specially tweaked for them.

As a brief summary, this program easily performs _tens or hundreds of thousands_ of FFTs to compute optimal paths in a stochastic graph. The graph is a road network, and each road requires a convolution of the travel time distribution and the arrival time vectors. These are not simple 1-shot convolutions as they have inter-dependencies—the details are difficult to summarize here, but you can find them in the linked paper & the nested references. The elements in these vectors have cross-dependencies on neighboring vectors, and as such, FFTs need to be performed in a particular manner—it is, in a sense, a manifestation of stochastic dynamic programming (DP).

I don't think it does in cases like this feature request. This is certainly too niche for a standard. ndarray methods: we don't want any more, adding a new method will be highly exceptional. Functions are preferred.

For functions, they should at least be:
1. widely applicable

I just ran into this same issue, it was maddening.  I narrowed it down to two cases:

# Unusual Behavior Example

**The first and last elements of the resulting "c" array are unitialized memory and will just contain whatever values happen to be in RAM at the moment:**  

```
import numpy as np

a = np.array([0,1,0])
b = np.array([1,1,1])

addCondition = np.where(a != 0, True, False)
c = np.add(a, b, where=addCondition)
```

# Fixed Example

**If I initialize the array first, I get what I expected (when the condition is False, just use the element from the first array instead of adding both):**

```
import numpy as np

a = np.array([0,1,0])
b = np.array([1,1,1])

addCondition = np.where(a != 0, True, False)
c = np.array(a)
np.add(a, b, out=c, where=addCondition)
```
Since numpy==2.4.0 use of `where` without `out` will warn. Closing.

Hello, I just wanted to add that this is something I ran into, and it cost me a day of work as I tried to trace the steps of what was going wrong in some code I had written. Someone smarter than me probably could've figured it out faster, but I figured maybe my experience as a less-than-genius user of numpy might be valuable.

The issue, of course, was that I didn't realize that numpy.cov() essentially uses a default of 1 for ddof. Not only was the behavior different from what I expected (which was the simple statistic, the same as numpy.var), the use of "None" as the real default implied to me at first glance that the default behavior **was** to do what I expected, which was ddof=0. Reading through the docs now the behavior does makes sense as written, but you have to interpret the behavior of the bias keyword as well to understand what is going on. Because I didn't look closely enough, I moved onto other things and it took me a while to circle back.

The changelog for this inconsistency goes all the way back to the early days of numpy, it looks like. The variance function was added first with ddof, and then covariance was added by a different developer using "bias", which is the convention in scipy as well. A third developer, seeking to unify the two, added the ddof argument to covariance but gave it a default of "None" so it didn't change the default behavior.

Because this is a problem that can't be solved by changing the behavior, I'd like to suggest a twofold solution to numpy.cov:


1. Change the default of ddof to 1
2. Include a warning when neither are specified

Because this doesn't change the default behavior or the hierarchy between the "ddof" and "bias" keywords, I don't think it would break any existing code and would make the default behavior a lot more clear to someone like me. I actually mentioned this to several friends at work who were horrified and found similar bugs in their own code because they didn't specify ddof. While the warnings would be ugly, it might just save a lot of users from headaches down the line.

For reference,  a bit of digging reveals that this discussion goes back to at least 2010 with a discussion on the NumPy-Discussion mailing list. https://www.mail-archive.com/numpy-discussion@scipy.org/msg27657.html 

On that thread a number of important questions were asked about the correct approach to implement this by Bruce Southey.

> Typical questions that come to mind are:
> 1) Should a user be warned that the input is a masked array?
> 2) Should histogram count the number of masked values?
> 3) What is the expected output when normed=True?
> 4) What type of array should be the weights and bin arguments?
> 5) What is the dimensions of the weight and bin arguments since it only needs to have the number of bins? 
> 6) If the input array is masked should the weight and bins arguments also be masked arrays when applicable? If so, what happens if the masks are in different locations between arrays?

Given the complexity of this, I'd therefore propose that masked arrays should ideally raise a ValueError here, and at least warn the user if it is called with a masked array

I think we might be open to changing the implementation to use `asanyarray`, with a set of tests to demonstrate the different error modes around matching sizes, mask mismatch, and what happens to `Nan`. Hopefully the change would give some thought to point (6).

Some suggested approaches to the questions above:
1. Most users of masked arrays would expect this to just work, so no warning is needed
2. by default the count will be the number of unmasked variables. A later extension would be to allow optionally for the count to be the total size of the array using an additional argument 
3. I think the output with normed=True (now called density) should be consistent with the count, so see (2)
4. Weights can be an unmasked array or a masked one, Bins should be an int or sequence but should not be masked (error).
5. as now weights need to be same shape as a. bins - same shape as currently
6. if shape is masked and any points are masked the mask should match the input array. If unmasked, print a warning that applying the mask from the input data to the weights.

as for NaN. If masked, and the mask is respected (i.e. ignored) then should not be an issue. If an unmasked array has NaN in it, or a masked array has points which are NaN that are NOT masked, then this should remain an error as at present (although a more helpful error perhaps can be returned)

I can see that this is error is unexpected, and pretty annoying to deal with. But technically speaking, this isn't a regression, because this issue also existed prior to 2.2; it just wasn't reported as such. The `np.linalg.inv` stubs itself haven't changed (functionally) since 2021 ([src](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/commit/ff80d911d2ef3644b658cdb003f8fff37b5b101e#diff-5424f0cc3e9875e487091f53b666fc98f6acdb7ae77752bc0ec0d6ceed55c99aR83-R88)).

If you look at the `np.linalg.inv` stub definition ([src](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/a48fb8562cce7e564f50f84f3717621b08edf490/numpy/linalg/_linalg.pyi#L160-L165)), you'll see that the return types are pretty broad:

```pyi
@overload
def inv(a: _ArrayLikeInt_co) -> NDArray[float64]: ...
@overload
def inv(a: _ArrayLikeFloat_co) -> NDArray[floating]: ...
@overload
def inv(a: _ArrayLikeComplex_co) -> NDArray[complexfloating]: ...
```

And while I fully agree that this can be annoying, I don't consider this to be a bug. It is valid to say that passing a `float64` array to `np.linalg.inv` results in a `floating` array. Clearly, it would be better if in that case it would return a `float64` array, rather than a `floating` one, but just because there's room for improvement, doesn't mean that it's a bug. So instead, I see this as a feature request (and a very reasonable one at that).

Note that most of the other `np.linalg` functions also have awkwardly broad return types ([src](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/a48fb8562cce7e564f50f84f3717621b08edf490/numpy/linalg/_linalg.pyi#L160-L165)). So when addressing this, it'd make sense to address these other functions as well.

This looks like a separate thing from the topic in this issue, and not a good idea to do wholesale. `skip_file_prefixes` may sometimes be useful, and sometimes just a more cumbersome and verbose way of achieving the same thing - it depends on code structure.

> skip_file_prefixes may sometimes be useful, and sometimes just a more cumbersome and verbose way of achieving the same thing - it depends on code structure.

From my point-of-view it's a better, less error-prone construction. Can you point to a specific example where you'd prefer to use `stacklevel`?

IMO the goal with `stacklevel` is to make sure warnings are generated with context in user code. To get that right, you need to either analyze the code or, more likely, trigger the warning and manually adjust the stacklevel so the warning context shows up in user code. If someone ever refactors the code so the stacklevel changes, they also need to adjust the warning.

Here's what I mean:

```python
# my_package/library.py
import warnings

def code_that_generates_warning():
    warnings.warn("warning!", UserWarning, stacklevel=4)

def library_function():
    code_that_generates_warning()

def main():
    library_function()
```

Here's what we see when we call the `main` function in a prompt or a file named `test_library.py`

```
goldbaum at Nathans-MBP in ~/Documents/test
○  python
Python 3.14.0 (main, Nov  6 2025, 14:16:12) [Clang 17.0.0 (clang-1700.4.4.1)] on darwin
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> from my_package.library import main
>>> main()
<python-input-1>:1: UserWarning: warning!
>>> exit

goldbaum at Nathans-MBP in ~/Documents/test
○  python test_library.py
/Users/goldbaum/Documents/test/test_library.py:2: UserWarning: warning!
  main()
```

The users have context for what code they wrote is generating the warning. Great! 

But what happens if someone refactors or adds a new calling site for `code_that_generates_warning` with a different call stack? For the latter, suddenly there's no unique calling site. For the former, you need very careful tests of your warnings.

What does all this look like with `skip_file_prefixes`? The warnings call would look like this:

```python
_warn_skips = (os.path.dirname(__file__),)

def code_that_generates_warning():
    warnings.warn("warning!", UserWarning, skip_file_prefixes=_warn_skips)
```

And everything works exactly as it did before, but now the warning code doesn't have to be adjusted if there's ever a refactor and `code_that_generates_warning` doesn't need logic to calculate the `stacklevel` based on the call stack above it. Not that anyone does the dynamic `stacklevel` calculation. Mostly there are a bunch of warnings in NumPy that give users context outside of their own code.

> Can you point to a specific example where you'd prefer to use `stacklevel`?

The default example in the CPython docs is a deprecation warning right above a public function. That's just cleaner with `stacklevel=2` and can't really go wrong. 

I am sure there are other cases where `stacklevel` is equivalent or better, because a tuple of absolute path to file names constructed with `__file__` is a pretty poor API: can also be broken by  a refactor as soon as it contains more than just the current file, makes one wonder if it's robust with editable installs etc. when .py files are pulled in via import hooks, or say everything is compiled into a `.exe` with a freezing tool.

And you may have cases where you want to use both at once. The docs anticipate this, they say: _"When prefixes are supplied, `stacklevel` is implicitly overridden to be `max(2, stacklevel)`."_

> I am sure there are other cases where stacklevel is equivalent or better, because a tuple of absolute path to file names constructed with __file__ is a pretty poor API: can also be broken by a refactor as soon as it contains more than just the current file, makes one wonder if it's robust with editable installs etc. when .py files are pulled in via import hooks, or say everything is compiled into a .exe with a freezing tool.

You don't need to go through `__file__`, you could set it to the package root, for example. That avoids the issue with refactoring. 

I'll have to look to see what happens with e.g. pyoxidizer.

IMO even where it's equivalent it's still less clear to use stacklevel and stacklevel still has the issue with requiring careful tests or careful refactoring.

also hitting this with `np.array_split` (same underlying issue). the stubs define:

```python
def array_split(
    ary: _ArrayLike[_ScalarT],
    indices_or_sections: _ShapeLike,
    axis: SupportsIndex = ...,
) -> list[NDArray[_ScalarT]]: ...
```

opened a PR with a fix: #30450

the fix adds a `_SupportsSplitOps` protocol that matches objects with `swapaxes` and `__getitem__` methods (like `pandas.DataFrame`). the protocol-based overload is placed first so it matches before the generic `ArrayLike` fallback:

```python
@type_check_only
class _SupportsSplitOps(Protocol):
    def swapaxes(self, axis1: Any, axis2: Any, copy: Any = ...) -> Any: ...
    def __getitem__(self, key: Any, /) -> Any: ...

_SplitableT = TypeVar("_SplitableT", bound=_SupportsSplitOps)

@overload
def array_split(
    ary: _SplitableT,
    indices_or_sections: _ShapeLike,
    axis: SupportsIndex = 0,
) -> list[_SplitableT]: ...
```

tested with `ty` type checker - reduces type errors from 43 to 28 on my codebase, with dataframe splits now correctly typed as `list[DataFrame]`.

I spent some time tracing the origin and usage of `npymath.ini` and `mlib.ini`. These files are pkg-config like metadata for the `npymath` C library, but they use a custom format rather than standard `.pc` files. They were introduced around 2009 and appear to have been part of the old Bento build system, which has been unmaintained for many years. While Meson still generates and installs them under `numpy/_core/lib/npy-pkg-config/`, I couldn’t find any place in the current NumPy codebase where they are actually read or used, neither by Python code, C/C++ code, nor by Meson itself. The only recent change was a mechanical move during the `_core` rename, not a functional update. Given that modern NumPy consumers rely on Meson dependencies, standard pkg-config files, or CMake configs, these `.ini` files appear to be leftover build artifacts. I just stumbled across this issue.

A common pattern in CSV files is for the column names to be in a comment.  `genfromtxt` allows this possibility when `names=True`.  It gets the names from the _first_ comment that it encounters (after skipping the `n` header lines if `skip_header=n` was given) before processing any actual rows of data.  If it doesn't find any initial comments, it gets the names from the first row of data.

For example, when read with `names=True`, all of the following produce the same array, with field names `Color`, `Type`, `Origin`, and `Stolen`:

```
Color Type Origin Stolen
Red Sports Domestic Yes
Red Sports Domestic No
Yellow Sports Domestic No
```

```
# Color Type Origin Stolen
Red Sports Domestic Yes
Red Sports Domestic No
Yellow Sports Domestic No
```

```
# Color Type Origin Stolen
# foo bar
Red Sports Domestic Yes
Red Sports Domestic No
Yellow Sports Domestic No
```

I think it would make more sense to take the names from the _last_ comment before the data begins.   I don't think I've ever seen a CSV file that had additional comments between a commented list of field names and the first row of data. This is the second issue in the list of issues when the "oldest" option is selected.  Perhaps with some concrete proposals, we can start working on closing it.

Some options:

1. Close as "won't fix".  Users that need a different behavior will have to use `skip_header` if they know in advance how many lines to skip, or use a different library, or write their own text reader.

2. Add more options to the existing `names` parameter.  Instead of the flexibility  of `names=True`, the new options are more explicit about where to find the column names:

   * `names=LAST_INITIAL_COMMENT` :
          Names are taken from the *last* initial comment ("initial" meaning at the top of the file, before any actual data).
          An error is raised if no initial comments are found.
   * `names=FIRST_NONCOMMENT` :
          Names are taken from the first noncommented line.

   (The literal tokens that indicate these behaviors are placeholders, with actual values to be determined--maybe something enum-like. String literals are not ideal because the current behavior is to get the field names from the string when a string is given.)

3. Add a new parameter: `commented_names`.  It is ignored if `names` is not `True`.  The values accepted by the new parameter and resulting behavior are:

   * `commented_names=None` :
     Default (current) behavior
   * `commented_names=True` :
     Names are taken from the *last* initial comment.
     An error is raised if no initial comments are found.
   * `commented_names=False` :
     Names are taken from the first noncommented line.

   (This option is a different way of providing the same possible behaviors as in the second option.  Same functionality, different spelling.)

Note: In all cases where the function gets the names from the file, the described behavior is applied after the number of lines indicated by `skip_header` have been skipped.

Any preferences?  Any other options to consider?

I lean towards option 2, but the problem is how to create the values LAST_INITIAL_COMMENT and FIRST_NONCOMMENT.  Some sub-options for option 2:

1)  Use the literal strings "last_initial_comment" and "first_noncomment".  Normally a string is expected to contain the comma-separated names, so this overloads the use of the string type in an awkward way, but it seems unlikely that any user will already be using one of these strings as the single field name in a file.
    This is probably the most concise API.
    To make it even less likely that the overloaded use of string type could cause a problem, a prefix could be required, e.g. "option:last_initial_comment" and "option:first_noncomment", but that makes it more verbose.
2)  An `enum` makes sense, but that requires that the `enum` "class" be attached to a public namespace.  A verbose name for that class could be `GenFromTxtNamesOptions`, and I doubt we want that in the top-level `numpy` namespace.  A bit of a hack would be to make it an attribute of `genfromtxt`, perhaps called `options`.  So a call of `genfromtxt` might be

        x = genfromtxt('foo.txt', names=genfromtxt.options.first_noncomment)

    or

        x = genfromtxt('foo.txt', names=genfromtxt.options.last_initial_comment)

    This avoids the overloading of the string type, but it is much more verbose, and requires a longer explanation in the docstring.

The issue you're encountering with the matrix multiplication on Windows in NumPy versions 2.0.0 and 2.0.1 appears to be related to the behavior of the underlying BLAS/LAPACK libraries, specifically OpenBLAS. This issue manifests as inconsistent failures in matrix multiplication operations involving large matrices, with mismatches occurring in a seemingly random pattern. 
Possible Causes:-
1. OpenBLAS Issues: Since the problem is observed with NumPy versions using OpenBLAS, there could be bugs or precision issues in the OpenBLAS library.
2. Numerical Precision: Handling of large numbers in floating-point arithmetic can sometimes lead to precision errors, especially if optimizations in the BLAS library affect the calculations.

Suggested Solutions and Workarounds
1. Use a Stable NumPy Version: If possible, use NumPy 1.26.4 or any version before 2.0.0 where this issue does not occur.
2. Switch to Another BLAS Implementation: Instead of OpenBLAS, try using MKL (Intel Math Kernel Library) if feasible. MKL is known for better numerical stability and performance, particularly on Intel architectures.

```
import numpy as np

def test():
    # Test whether matrix multiplication involving a large matrix always gives the same answer
    x = np.arange(500000, dtype=np.float64)
    src = np.vstack((x, -10*x)).T
    matrix = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]])

    expected = np.vstack((-10*x, x)).T  # src @ matrix
    
    mismatches = np.zeros(500, int)
    retries = 5  # Number of retries to handle sporadic failures

    for i in range(len(mismatches)):
        for attempt in range(retries):
            result = src @ matrix
            mismatches[i] = (~np.isclose(result, expected)).sum()
            if mismatches[i] == 0:
                break
            else:
                print(f"Retry {attempt + 1}: {mismatches[i]} mismatching elements in multiplication #{i}")

        if mismatches[i] != 0:
            print(f"Final {mismatches[i]} mismatching elements in multiplication #{i}")

test()
```
This function will attempt the matrix multiplication up to 5 times if mismatches are found, printing the number of mismatching elements after each attempt. This is not a perfect solution but can help mitigate the impact of the issue in the short term.

What is the problem. The failure is in this line [1]: 

```

with `phi` is a numpy scalar computed from outputs of `np.eig`. The remainder assumes that `phi` is real and emits a ComplexWarning otherwise. Currently, this line _sometimes_ fails: [2]. Note that Stefan asked for a reproducer [3], in 2023.


[1] https://github.com/scikit-image/scikit-image/blob/959c3b8500cb212dabf3e0ed594a8169d44a113a/src/skimage/measure/fit.py#L905

[3] https://github.com/scikit-image/scikit-image/issues/7013#issuecomment-1583203321

- scikit-image code assumes that eigenvalues are real;
- this sometimes breaks (because actually no, they are not always real)
- scikit-image considers this a bug


Therefore, the fix is two-fold:

Step 1: replace

```
eig_vals, eig_vecs = np.linalg.eig(M)
```

with

```
eig_vals, eig_vecs = np.linalg.eig(M)
if eig_vals.imag != 0:

eig_vecs = eig_vecs.real
```

I cloned the NumPy source, built it locally, and started testing the reproducer. While doing so, I noticed that the behavior differs depending on the Python version used.

With the latest NumPy release (2.3.5):
* On **Python <= 3.12**, I can reliably reproduce the crash using a multiprocessing setup.
* On **Python 3.13 and 3.14**, I cannot reproduce the issue — neither with multiprocessing nor with multithreading(with free-threaded interpreter).

After investigating this difference, I found the explanation.
* Python 3.13 introduced **PEP 683 (Immortal Objects)**, where certain objects are initialized with a special refcount that is unaffected by `Py_INCREF` or `Py_DECREF`.
* NumPy initializes `_PyArrayScalar_BoolValues` in `scalartypes.c.src` ([line 56](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/1ec4bd0f6031ae86a372394ea06e6e23ce90d3c1/numpy/_core/src/multiarray/scalartypes.c.src#L56)), and the initialization uses `PyObject_HEAD_INIT`.
* Starting with CPython 3.13, any object created using `PyObject_HEAD_INIT` receives the immortal refcount ([Include/object.h](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/a183a11db8bc2520c52814635de2df118d2d7e8c/Include/object.h#L128)), which effectively turns `np.True` and `np.False` into immortal objects.

This fully explains the observed behavior:
* On **Python >= 3.13**, the double evaluation in `PyArrayScalar_RETURN_BOOL_FROM_LONG` no longer causes refcount corruption because increment/decrement operations are no-ops for immortal objects.
* On **Python <= 3.12**, boolean scalar singletons are still regular reference-counted objects, so the race condition can corrupt their refcounts and trigger a crash.

Since NumPy 2.3.x still supports Python 3.12, I think it’s still worth fixing the macro as we discussed. For the test, I can reproduce the issue reliably using a multiprocessing setup on 3.12 — likely using multiprocessing.shared_memory to create a platform-agnostic buffer rather than relying on memmap semantics. That should provide a clean and deterministic reproducer.

I think it is because the test relies on `break_cycles` to clear references which just calls `gc.collect()`. If another thread has requested gc then that function is a no-op and doesn't break cycles. See https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/137682

I looked a little closer at the `numpy.random` races. I think we need to use critical sections in the Cython NumPy RNG implementation to make sure no new races are possible on the free-threaded build.

Basically, whenever the internal state of the RNG is read from or mutated, we need to take a critical section. Here's how I modified `RandomState.set_state`:

```
diff --git a/numpy/random/mtrand.pyx b/numpy/random/mtrand.pyx
index 8e7f437641..55cc7a3fd3 100644
--- a/numpy/random/mtrand.pyx
+++ b/numpy/random/mtrand.pyx
@@ -381,9 +381,13 @@ def set_state(self, state):
                     st['has_gauss'] = state[3]
                     st['gauss'] = state[4]

-        self._aug_state.gauss = st.get('gauss', 0.0)
-        self._aug_state.has_gauss = st.get('has_gauss', 0)
-        self._bit_generator.state = st
+        cdef double gauss = st.get('gauss', 0.0)
+        cdef int has_gauss = st.get('has_gauss', 0)
+
+        with cython.crticial_section(self):
+            self._aug_state.gauss = gauss
+            self._aug_state.has_gauss = has_gauss
+            self._bit_generator.state = st
```

Moving the `st.get` calls outside of the critical section avoids calling back into the CPython C API while the critical section is held.

This is working as expected: in Python, lists are mutable objects. When you write this:
```
ck1 = [[ck0]*n]*n
```
the result is that `ck1` contains `n` references to the same list, and when you modify that list, the modification is reflected in all references. Here's an example without NumPy:
```python
>>> L = [1]

>>> x = [L, L]

>>> x
[[1], [1]]

>>> L[0] = 2

>>> x
[[2], [2]]
```
If you don't want this behavior, you should avoid creating multiple references to the same list; for example in your code, you could use a list comprehension like this:
```python
ck1 = [[ck0 for i in range(n)] for j in range(n)]
```
(but then make sure not to make any in-place modifications of `ck0`, because you are still creating 49 references to it!)

The code was using both. For `np.MAXDIMS`, this was usually to store an int that would be saved in a "params" dict that could be used by python objects, but could also be translated to C code. The `NPY_MAXDIMS` macro was used in some C code for some of the operations in Pytensor. Where `NPY_MAXDIMS` was used in (python functions that create) C code, I switched to `NPY_RAVEL_AXIS`. It was an intentional change to make `start` a positional-only argument in the stubs. There are several reasons for this, and one of them is mentioned in the [release notes](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/releases/tag/v2.4.0rc1):

> Type-checkers will no longer accept calls to `numpy.arange` with
> `start` as a keyword argument. This was done for compatibility with
> the Array API standard. At runtime it is still possible to use
> `numpy.arange` with start as a keyword argument.

Another reason is that there is simply no way to fully and correctly express the callable signature otherwise.

Luckily, the fix is very easy: write `np.arange(0, stop=10, step=1)` instead of `np.arange(start=0, stop=10, step=1)` :).

The docstring is indeed not very clear, but the `__iadd__` operator does actually return an array; it is just that `value` is added in-place and then `self` is returned:
```
In [2]: a = np.arange(5.0)

In [3]: a.__iadd__(1)
Out[3]: array([1., 2., 3., 4., 5.])

In [4]: a
Out[4]: array([1., 2., 3., 4., 5.])
```

What I am pointing out is not whether `__iadd__` returns a value, but whether it is appropriate to express the return value as `self+=value`. At least in the Python language, `return self+=value` is not syntactically correct.

@r-devulap thoughts?

> x86-simd-sort is not working well for amd 7950x see https://github.com/intel/x86-simd-sort/issues/6

That issue was present on AMD Zen 4 CPUs due to the high latency of the `compressstore` instruction. I’m open to addressing it on Zen 4, but doing so would require building a dedicated build for that architecture and adding separate runtime dispatch. This essentially duplicates the simd-sort implementation and adds to code size. I’m not entirely sure  it’s worth the effort for a single CPU generation, especially since the problem no longer exists on Zen 5 and future processors. On Zen 5, vqsort and x86-simd-sort deliver very similar performance — see [this gist](https://gist.github.com/r-devulap/491bb311fa51c6c021cbae11c95cc323) for detailed numbers.

> the furure of x86-simd-sort is uncertain see https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/29694

Future of x86-simd-sort is pretty clear: it will move to NumPy namespace and will be supported going forward. 

> I understand that numpy is slowly adopting Google Highway simd infrastructure and hwy sort is already used on ARM (if I am not mistaken), so why not extend it to other platforms? hwy sort is designed for broader range of architecture.

This is a reasonable argument. However, Highway currently does not support index sorting for `np.argsort` and `np.argpartition`. If highway at some point implements these, then we could circle back and think about this. 

> it seems that it is faster to intel sort but I haven't tested myself (did not manage yet to make it work), see https://github.com/google/highway/tree/master/hwy/contrib/sort

That analysis is quite old and performance of x86-simd-sort pretty much matches that of vqsort and IIRC, it is better for some data types.

There is ongoing work to bring full sorting, including support for emulated half-precision and later argsort:

- https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/29829
- https://github.com/google/highway/pull/2737

Currently facing an issue related to compilation time on Highway, and we are working on it.

Note that `builtins.float`, `int`, and `bool`, also don't implement `__complex__`, because there simply is no need for it:

Constructing a `builtins.complex` from an object does not require a `__complex__` to be implemented, as long as it implements `__float__` or `__index__`. This can be seen in the [typeshed stubs for `builtins.complex`](https://github.com/python/typeshed/blob/94ffa6e3f512b491252a1d0674fef8a3f283534d/stdlib/builtins.pyi#L432-L469), for example. 

All of NumPy's floats, integers, and `bool`, implement the `__float__` method, and are therefore already convertible to `builtins.complex`. So adding a `__complex__` to them won't help with that.

The only use-case for `__complex__` I can think of is for custom complex-like types, like the ones in `complexfloating`. Otherwise, there you wouldn't be able to convert them to a `builtins.complex` without them losing the imaginary part, since `__float__` will ignore that.

Hi! I appreciate the motivation for this, but one data point: as proposed, this will make jax scalar type aliases (e.g. `jax.numpy.float32`, `jax.numpy.int32`, etc.) unusable as dtypes.

Some background: JAX made the choice early to not have distinct scalar type classes, but rather to represent scalars as 0-dimensional arrays. What this means is that when it comes to the `jax.numpy` API, we want `jnp.float32(0)` to be a function that returns a zero-dimensional `jax.Array`.

Ah! An opportunity to rant about static typing; don't mind if I do:

In static-typing jargon the `numpy.ndarray` class is called a [generic type](https://typing.python.org/en/latest/spec/generics.html). It has two (covariant) type parameters: One for the `.shape`, and another for `.dtype`. The shape type must be assignable to `tuple[int, ...]`, which includes any integer tuple. The dtype type (not a typo, and no pub intended) must be assignable to `np.dtype`, for obvious reasons. So if `a` is a one-dimensional `float64` array, it can be annotated as

```py
a: np.ndarray[tuple[int], np.dtype[np.float64]]
```

When you do something like

```py
a.shape = (1, 2, 3)
```

then `a` is no longer one-dimensional, but the type says it is. Type-checkers will allow you to pass `a` to a function that *only* accepts 1d arrays, otherwise it'll nuke the entire universe. But `a` is no longer one-dimensional, even though type-checkers are convinced that it is. So type-checkers are no longer to protect you from nuking the universe. And clearly, the same problems arise when you mutate `dtype` in-place.

> One naive question I have is how changing the `shape` attribute is more thread-unsafe than mutating the array data itself.

Concurrent mutation of the data (e.g. `array[2, 3]= 5`) can lead to funny results (you could call them incorrect, but that depends on your point of view). That is hard to debug and surprising, but one could argue this is the user responsibility.

But changing the `shape` in a concurrent thread can lead to a crash of the interpreter. A simple example:

* Two threads A and B are working on an array of shape `(10, 2)`. 
* Thread A wants to loop over the 2 dimensions of the array. It first reads the size of first dimension 0 (e.g. 10).
* A concurrent thread B resizes the array to shape `(2, 10)` 
* Thread A then reads the size of the second dimension. This was 2, but (because of the resize by thread B) has been updated to value 10.
* Thread A performs an iteration over the data of the array assuming the shape of the array `(10, 10)`. This leads to an `IndexError` if executed from the Python side, but can lead corruption of the the interpreter when executed from the C side.  (even when working full from the python side, there are some numpy methods not thread safe and can crash)

FWIW, in https://github.com/data-apis/array-api/pull/814#issuecomment-2430366279 I proposed the following semantics for `clip`:

> Let T be the data type of x. If there exists a value in T that is greater than or equal to min and less than or equal to max, then clip(x, min, max) returns (1) the smallest element in T that is greater than or equal to min if x < min, (2) the largest element in T that is less than or equal to max if x > max, or (3) x otherwise.
>
> In math notation, this becomes
>
> $$
> \mathrm{clip}(x,a,b):= {\arg\min}_{ t \in T\cap [a,b]} | t-x |
> $$

I think this definition is general enough to account for most (all?) corner cases of inputs. It is implementable for built-in types by first “snapping” the bounds to a representable value in T “in the right direction” and then doing the obvious min(max(…)) thing. For custom numeric types  such as Decimal or Fraction, could just throw an error.

We don't really mention it much because most people generally expect this property of most of our functions anyways. Nondeterminism is actually hard to accomplish! You have to introduce concurrency carelessly or query the operating system for environmental state. We don't do a lot of concurrency, and where we do, we try to be careful because people do expect this property (or rely on libraries that do). We query the environment in a handful of places (e.g. `np.random.default_rng()`), and we do document (lack of) determinism there.

FWIW, with all due respect to @nickodell who provided that answer, I'm not sure that actual nondeterministic randomness is that popular of an option in quicksort implementations. Deterministic pseudorandomness sometimes is (pseudorandomness helps average-case performance in tie-breaking without introducing nondeterminism). I guess some particularly quick-and-dirty implementations might pull the OS's `rand()` function for this purpose with nondeterministic seeding. That one _could_ do any number of silly things implementing quicksort doesn't obligate us to disclaim them, I don't think.

Sometimes people come to our documentation with a particular frame of ideas in their head, and the documentation doesn't serve them well immediately. Sometimes, we judge that that frame is pretty rare, so we don't feel a strong need to cater to it in the documentation itself. We can't document every possible property of our code that someone might ask about it; usability matters. Some questions are best handled by searchable answers on StackOverflow; it complements our documentation. Our documentation is good at serving some purposes, and StackOverflow is good at others. All I'm trying to say is that I think this is the latter. One question appearing on StackOverflow isn't strong evidence that we must add something to our documentation.

That is how things have developed over the years, the changes just make it explicit. Default may or may not be stable, the idea is to use something fast that doesn't use too much memory.

Numeric just called the C standard `qsort()` routine, which may in fact use OS randomness underneath on some implementations (old and bad ones; the classic [Engineering a sort function](https://web.archive.org/web/20140116101822/http://citeseer.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.14.8162) from 1993 quickly moves on from that alternative); determinacy isn't part of any of the relevant standards.
