It's not the NPY format so much as the pickling. When you have to use pickled objects, you generally have to use the same version of the library providing the object on both sides. Pickling involves recording a blob of data in data types that `pickle` knows about (e.g. builtin types like `list`s and `tuple`s and `float`s and `bytes`) and a reference (by fully-qualified name) to a function to reconstruct the full object from your library. When a library reorganizes its code, as we did in the 2.0 transition, the location of the reconstruction function might change. I believe we left aliases at the old location of these functions such that 1.x pickles can be loaded in 2.x, but when 2.x makes a pickled array, it uses the current location, which did not exist in 1.x. I.e. we have backwards compatibility for pickles (something most libraries don't bother with) but not forwards compatibility. We have never promised forwards compatibility, I don't think (and certainly not for the pickled option), and I'm not sure we're about to start.

If you want to share files between 1.x and 2.x, you will need to avoid pickling at all costs.

If your data is actually just a dictionary of "ordinary" arrays (e.g. not `dtype=object` arrays), consider using `np.savez()` instead. `np.save()` works on numpy arrays, not arbitrary objects. When it's given an arbitrary object, it will convert it to a 0-dim `dtype=object` array with its solve value being that object, and save that. Because it is `dtype=object`, it must use pickle. So you are making an `.npy` file that is really just a pickle with a fancy header. You'd run into the same error just by use `pickle.save()/pickle.load()` on `data`.

`np.savez()`, on the other hand, if given named arrays will make a ZIP file where each file in there is an NPY file of each array. So if `data` is just a `dict` with strings as keys and `ndarray`s with the usual set of concrete `dtype`s, then that will work for you without pickling.

If you need to just make it work once, you can check https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/28340 which has some patterns that should work at the end. Otherwise, as said, avoiding pickle is best of course.

I ran into this when attempting to use `matplotlib.pyplot.hist2d` to plot a heatmap of data indexed by timestamp. I suspect this is a very common use-case for seeing how histograms evolve over time.

Here is a minimal reproducer; `plt.hist2d` calls `np.histogramdd` directly, so this is just cutting out the middleman:

```python
import numpy as np
x = np.array([
    np.datetime64('2005-02-25T03:30', 's'),
])
y = np.ones(x.shape)
np.histogramdd([x, y])
```

Currently, I can work around this by setting `bins` manually, but it's very tedious and it took significant debugging to figure out _why_ `matplotlib` couldn't handle this.

For future readers, the bug here is that `np.atleast_2d([x,y])` returns an array with `dtype=object`:

https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/e468d88310a65c16ba9181b06462f78400e80257/numpy/lib/_histograms_impl.py#L981-L987

Then that array's `.min()` returns a native Python `datetime.datetime` object, which results in an exception when `np.isfinite` is called:

https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/e468d88310a65c16ba9181b06462f78400e80257/numpy/lib/_histograms_impl.py#L1017

https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/e468d88310a65c16ba9181b06462f78400e80257/numpy/lib/_histograms_impl.py#L315-L316

People piling on this issue: it is a problem with the BLAS implementation used by NumPy. You can use `np.show_runtime()` after installing `threadpoolctl` or `python -m threadpoolctl -i numpy` to get the information, any comments without that information are not really helpful.

The situation, as far I can tell, is this:
- For Accelerate the problem was "solved" in #29223 by ignoring FPE. Accelerate is the version of BLAS used by NumPy via the PyPI wheels for macos-arm64, i.e. `pip install numpy==2.3.3`.
- OpenBLAS 0.3.30 uses SME but was not included in #29223. I think this is the BLAS implementation intalled by default in `conda install numpy`
- Some previous version of OpenBLAS may not have the problem since it does not use SME, but no-one with an M4 has done the work to tell us which one (hint: `conda install "libopenblas==0.3.29"` might be a start).

We might want to widen the check in blasutils to non-acclerate https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/201bbb28e0daf1eb60082a0dc4af9dd8273425d0/numpy/_core/src/common/blas_utils.c#L70, but someone with an M4 would have to verify the fix.

To give a more concrete example; consider a simple function that transforms a Python builtin scalar into a `numpy.generic` one:

For the sake of simplicity, let's limit ourselves to just the numeric scalar types.

# Stubs with incompatible overlapping overloads

```python
from typing import overload
import numpy as np

@overload
def scalar(x: bool, /) -> np.bool: ...  # ok
@overload
def scalar(x: int, /) -> np.int_: ...  # wrong
@overload
def scalar(x: float, /) -> np.float64: ...  # wrong
@overload
def scalar(x: complex, /) -> np.complex128: ...  # wrong
```

At first glance, it doesn't look like there's anything wrong with this.
And some simple tests would show that it's working as expected, e.g.:

- `reveal_type(scalar(True))` gives `np.bool` ✅ 
- `reveal_type(scalar(42))` gives `np.int_` ✅ 
- `reveal_type(scalar(1 / 137))` gives `np.float64` ✅ 
- `reveal_type(scalar((-1) ** .5))` gives `np.complex128` ✅ 

But directly passing a constant to a function isn't something that's done very often.
In practice, we almost always pass a variable, which aren't limited to be an instance of a specific *class*:

reveal_type(x_py)
x_np = scalar(x_py)
reveal_type(x_np)
```

But that's clearly wrong: `x_np` could also be a `np.bool`, a `np.int_`, or a `np.float64`!

## Why is it wrong?

The source of this issue lies in what the [typing spec](https://typing.readthedocs.io/en/latest/spec/special-types.html#special-cases-for-float-and-complex) calls "Special cases for `float` and `complex`":

> Python’s numeric types `complex`, `float` and `int` are not subtypes of each other, but to support common use cases, the type system contains a straightforward shortcut: when an argument is annotated as having type `float`, an argument of type `int` is acceptable; similar, for an argument annotated as having type `complex`, arguments of type `float` or `int` are acceptable.

So in other words: type-checkers must assume that `issubclass(int, float) and issubclass(float, complex)`, even though this isn't the case at runtime, nor are they type-compatible (i.e. in the way that protocols can be).

This makes it impossible to distinguish between e.g. "float | int" and "float", as they are treated the same.

NumPy APIs are designed to work with NumPy arrays, not scipy sparse array objects, and in general you should not expect the two to be compatible. When working with `scipy.sparse` objects, you should use `scipy.sparse` functions to ensure correct results. For example:
```python
>>> v.dot(w).shape
()
```

The reason for the output you're seeing is that `np.dot` casts its input to arrays, and `v` and `w` when passed to `np.asarray` become scalar arrays of type `object`:
```python
>>> np.asarray(v)
array(<COOrdinate sparse array of dtype 'float64'
	with 1 stored elements and shape (3,)>, dtype=object)
```
`np.dot` of two scalars is equivalent to multiplication, and `v * w` returns a length 3 sparse array.

This casting behavior is a decision made by the `scipy.sparse` implementation (via the `__array__` method), likely to avoid unintentional conversion of sparse arrays to full dense arrays.

After diving into the FFT code in _pocketfft.py and the way shape and axes are paired, it turns out that the current forward‐order for irfftn is intentional and must not be flipped. 1. In irfftn the code first does n-point complex→complex FFTs in exactly the order the user passed in axes[:-1], pairing each transform with the matching entry in the user’s shape[:-1]. 2. Finally it does the complex→real transform on axes[-1] with shape[-1]. If you reversed the loop you would also have to reverse–or otherwise remap–the shape entries to the axes you’re touching. That change would silently break every existing irfftn call that uses s/axes (even when axes are unique). Given that the only time “order matters” is when you do silly things like repeat axes, and NumPy does not guarantee well‐defined behavior in that edge case, the current implementation is correct. We should leave irfftn alone and, if anything, clarify in the documentation that repeated axes + s is not a supported use case.

I think you answered your question yourself. In the first case you are using multiple threads, in the second you are limiting the computation to one thread. As explained [elsewhere](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/29873#issuecomment-3394919165), it is tricky to control cumulative error. You did not state what operating system you are using, nor where you got NumPy, nor what version you are using as requested when opening an issue so it is difficult to say more. What does this show? 
```
$ pip install threadpoolctl
$ python -c "import numpy; print(numpy.show_runtime())"  
```

What you are seeing is not a bug in NumPy but a consequence of floating-point reductions being non-associative and the fact that under mpirun your BLAS library (OpenBLAS, Intel MKL, etc.) may be spawning different thread(s) and/or using a different reduction tree.

Even though you only launched one MPI rank, mpirun often propagates environment settings (like OMP_NUM_THREADS, MKL_NUM_THREADS, or internal affinity flags) that cause your underlying BLAS to parallelize the dot product differently.

Different thread counts or reduction orders lead to tiny differences in the rounding of a long sum. A difference on the order of 10⁻¹⁵ is exactly what you would expect from two different summation orders.

If you need bit-identical reproducibility, you can:
• Force BLAS to run single-threaded: export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1
• Use a compensated summation algorithm (e.g. Kahan) in Python.
• Perform your own reduction in Python exactly in the same sequence.

Otherwise, rest assured that both results (2278.2443714923875 vs 2278.2443714923884) are correct to within floating-point precision.

TL;DR: Do you have a compelling use case that would convince us it is worth the effort and complications and often impedance mismatch threading brings? Please share it to convince us this is worth it. 

This idea comes up from time to time. The problem is where to put the proper level of granularity when distributing work to threads. NumPy itself does not have many complicated algorithms that would provide natural groupings into threaded functions. Where possible, NumPy does delegate such work to BLAS libraries, which can use multiple cores. The low-level operations (often implemented as ufuncs) like `add` or `multiply` are typically combined in higher level user code, and rarely used alone. Here is a concrete example: `c = a + b; d = c * c`. Rather than 
- executing `a + b` in threaded code, 
- waiting for all the threads and gathering the answer into `c`
- calculating `c * c` in threaded code and finally 
- waiting for all the threads and gathering the answer into `d`
 
it would be better to do something like this, where the decorator looks at the operation in its entirety, breaks it into blocks, and executes in threads
```
@threadme
def func(a, b):
    c = a + b
    return c * c
```

Well, it turns out this is exactly what [Numba](https://numba.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user/parallel.html) does (and does quite well), so we prefer to delegate to them. I think PyTorch also has a mode where it will analyze and speed up code.

Not only that, but threading brings a whole level of new problems. How to control the number of threads used, when sometimes code can be run on many processes? What should the chunk size be? How does the threading model interact with the different BLAS implementations NumPy can be built with, or with native Python threads?

So given all that, we prefer to Keep It Simple.

I am not sure immediately if there are some internal calculations that should maybe always use float64 at least (because they are related to the length of an array, so need full float64 mantissa to be pretty correct).

This indeed seems tricky to get right: the output of  `get_virtual_index=lambda n, quantiles: (n - 1) * quantiles` is an array with virtual indices `virtual_indexes` that is used in two ways (roughly):

* `floor(virtual_indexes)` and `ceil(virtual_indices)` are indices of the two data points (in the sorted data) used for interpolation
* `g= virtual_indexes % 1` is used as a factor to interpolate between the two data points

We can use `np.interp` (or some other way) to calculate the value of  `(n - 1) * quantiles` without overflows, but the result has to be in float64 (at least higher than float16 which is not enough). Then also `g` will be `float64` and the final result of `np.quantile` is `(1-g)*y[j] + g*y[j+1]` which will also be `float64`. This is not ideal since we would like to have the output of `np.quantile(float16_array, [0, .5, .99])` to be float16. On the other hand, `np.quantile([0, 1, 3], [0])` is also promoted to float64. 

We could downcast `g` to the dtype of the input array. (since `g` is in the 0 to 1 range that seems fine), but that might break cases with integer input.

Oh we definitely want symbol suffixes, because in a stack with numpy and scipy we use a mix of LP64 and ILP64 APIs. There's no good control over that with wheels, and without suffixes it's too easy to get symbol clashes.

I agree but can we hope to have ecosystem-wide recommendations to adopt one vs the other in the long run? That would avoiding linking to two different OpenBLAS copies for a typical scipy runtime env. This would be both helpful to reduce the size of deployed Python apps (particularly important on edge or WASM and more generally for people with not so great network connections). It would also help reduce debugging complexity in case two OpenBLASes interact in the same Python program (I can imagine spin-waiting threads causing performance problems when calling successively one OpenBLAS implementation and then the other in a tight loop.

A couple of thoughts there:
- Long-term I think we want ILP64
- However, ILP64 support is currently fairly immature all around (in both BLAS libraries and in downstream code, e.g. not all external libs that SciPy vendors fully support it, like SuperLU) compared to LP64
- There is also the problem that SciPy re-exports the LP64 API through `scipy.linalg.cython_blas`, so that will always be needed
- The NumPy decision to start shipping ILP64 by default in 1.22.0 (IIRC that was the version) was quite premature and will make it a long-term endeavor to use only a single BLAS library in wheels.
  - It's hard to go back now though, because it's hard to know who is relying on that ILP64 support now for dealing with large matrices
  - I'm not sure it's actually impossible. I could be convinced otherwise I think. As you point out, smaller binary size of deployed stack is an important argument. Probably significantly more important than supporting the "doesn't fit in 32-bit integers" crowd (it's anyway not possible to write code that is portable to conda-forge and Linux distros for such corner cases). So we may consider it if and when we can ship wheels that can rely on `scipy-openblas32`/`64`
- To end up with a single shared library in the end, what we need is for that library to support both LP64 and ILP64 symbols. MKL and Accelerate already do this; reference BLAS has now settled on the `64_` symbol suffix so should be able to start shipping a single library in the future. Most importantly, we need an OpenBLAS build with both sets of symbols. That's still going to take a while.
- WASM is an easier case, because it's 32-bit: we should definitely use LP64 only there

I'm not sure if this can be regarded as a bug.  To guarantee results across platforms NumPy would have to commit to a specific accumulation order for the terms in the dot product *and* eschew the use of FMA instructions.  This would preclude the use of any external BLAS libraries and likely result in worse accuracy when FMA instructions are available.

The transformation of multiply-adds (a*b + c) to a single (and more accurate) FMA is explicitly allowed by IEEE 754 (i.e., a C compiler can do it without `-ffast-math`) and will absolutely impact results of dot products since they're just FMA chains.

I think I agree; enforcing reproducibility across platforms at the sacrifice of performance is likely not in the best interest of NumPy as a whole.

That being said, I think that functions that depend on BLAS libraries should have a note in their documentation that clearly states that there is no guarantee of exact reproducibility across operating systems, and perhaps a link to a section that describes how it can be compiled to ensure reproducibility across platforms.

If we had such a glaring bug, you should be able to show it with a more dissimilar result. Try something that outputs values that have a relative difference more than 2e-16.

The underlying issue is with your algorithm.  If you get vastly different results based on relative changes of 2e-16 to the inputs/intermediates then *your algorithm is numerically unstable*.  Forget floating point, forget different architectures, the issue is with the algorithm.  In general, uses of `floor`, `ceil`, and `round` are very often a cause for suspicion in numerical code as they are functions which can amplify a small relative difference into a massive one.  Relying on them never ends well (and I speak from experience here).

1. We already have the `warn_on_overflow` warning, it comes in the [errstate](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.seterr.html). But currently errstate does not always kick in on integer ufunc and scalar operations.
2. Rather than just reductions, we should check all ufunc and scalar ops.
3. See (1)
4. The problematic impact is the performance cost. In order to avoid any reduction in performance, the new code may need to duplicate all the older code on the ~22 ufuncs and a similar number of scalar options (there are a number of alternate loop implementations for each operation due to different SIMD options). This would preserve performance, but complicate the code base and make the runtime installation larger.

There are two possible approaches in general to triggering the warnings. One is to extend the `errstate` or decide to use it as-is without changing the dtypes. Another would be to have slower "user-friendly" built-in dtypes that would always error/warn on overflow or divide-by-0.

This is a large change that certainly needs a design discussion, if not a NEP.

## Potential Issues:

I think the reason is cache associativity conflicts. When your matrix is 100×100 with double precision (8 bytes), each row occupies exactly 800 bytes. This stride creates pathological cache behavior. Modern CPUs use 64-byte cache lines​ and each row stride of 800 bytes = 12.5 cache lines (not cleanly aligned)​

* In set-associative caches (typically 4-way to 16-way), memory addresses are mapped to cache sets using modular arithmetic based on the address​
* When multiple matrix rows are accessed (as happens during A @ A.T), elements from different rows with similar column indices compete for the same cache sets

But with 99x99 -> 99*8 = 792 bytes. 792 is not a "round" number in cache terms and distributes accesses more evenly across cache sets

I also suspect that **OpenBLAS changes algorithm** or probably uses **multi threading** when reaching matrices of size 100 or so but ***I have to confirm this***.

If we look at the matrix as a whole right, 800 * 100 (100x100 matrix) is 80000 and 80,000 is a round number that can cross:
* 64 KB or 128 KB L1/L2 cache boundary
* glibc malloc bin thresholds (so it allocates from a different pool)
* Page alignment boundaries → possible TLB misses

One improvement to the pattern would be to avoid having a live, operational `Generator` be the static, stored object. That's mildly error-prone, because if anyone calls any methods on it in the interim, you'll break the desired semantics. Rather, we might consider adding a function (not a method) that kind of works like `default_rng()`, except that it returns an opaque object that holds a `SeedSequence` and the `BitGenerator` type and will construct a fresh `Generator` from those two on request. When given a static seed like an integer (or a sequence of ints), then it just returns `SeedSequence(seed)` (and I think it should pass through a `SeedSequence` if one is passed, but I could be convinced that it should spawn). But if given a `Generator`, it will reach down and spawn from the underlying `SeedSequence` and use that spawned `SeedSequence`, which is now owned by this object. When you kick off the computation, you call this opaque object to get a fresh `Generator` and go.

The main problem with this scheme is mostly finding a name that's not super-confusing.

```python
from copy import deepcopy
from functools import partial

import numpy as np


def reusable_rng_factory(rng=None):
    if isinstance(rng, np.random.Generator):
        # Grab the BitGenerator and fall through to the next if clause
        rng = rng._bit_generator
    if isinstance(rng, np.random.BitGenerator):
        seed_seq = rng._seed_seq.spawn(1)[0]
        bg_type = type(rng)
        # Why the deepcopy? SeedSequence has some state concerning the number of spawns it has done.
        # To get the same starting state each time, we need 
        restorer = lambda seed: np.random.Generator(bg_type(deepcopy(seed)))
    else:
        seed_seq = np.random.SeedSequence(rng)
        restorer = lambda seed: np.random.default_rng(deepcopy(seed))
    # Obviously, this probably should be a real type with a name and docstrings, but this gets across the idea.
    # Basically opaque, with just a __call__ method for the API.
    return partial(restorer, seed_seq)


class MyFancyComputation:
    def __init__(self, rng=None):
        self._rng_factory = reusable_rng_factory(rng)

    def method(self):
        rng = self._rng_factory()
        x = rng.standard_normal(1000)
        ...
````

Forgot to respond to this. You do _not_ want to clone the `Generator` that is passed in. You must spawn a `Generator` from that `Generator` before you can clone a copy from it. The rule is [*Only clone it if you own it*](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/16988#issuecomment-1518037853). Otherwise, the original passed-in `Generator` will continue on _outside_ of the CV splitter (in this example) and generate correlated values with those used _inside_ of the CV splitter, and that is not what you want. The only things you want to be correlated are the things you deliberately designed to be correlated: multiple calls to the splitter.

Hi everybody, I'm surprised to hear that -1 in shapes for `np.load` ever worked. Back then when I worked on the NPY format, I created a version that explicitly allowed -1 in shapes, but it required some code to be added to handle the -1 and my suggestion was never merged.

With my experience nowadays I would recommend not to use -1 in a NPY array shape. Yes, it allows arbitrary big files without modifying the header at all, but comes with the catch that it's not possible to detect incomplete file transfers/copies. In my project [npy-append-array](https://github.com/xor2k/npy-append-array) (which supposedly broke with the latest numpy-2.3 release https://github.com/xor2k/npy-append-array/issues/12 which is probably unrelated to the issue described in this thread here), I handle the header rewrite on append problem like this:
1. By default, the header is rewritten on every append done to the file
2. The user can specify to have the header only rewritten on destruction of the append context, then it will only be rewritten once
3. There are some tools to fix the header in the postproduction by "recovering" a broken NPY file. By default, it will remove trailing content that is incompatible with the shape, but it can also be configured to zerofill to squeeze the last bytes out of the incomplete NPY file.

Thank you for inviting me to the discussion, I hope I could help!

The pre-2.3.0 behavior relied on another implementation detail/undefined behavior. `np.load()` only worked on these files when they were opened with an authentic `file` object so that `np.fromfile()` could be used, which reaches down to use the underlying OS file descriptor in the C level. We do compute the number of items to read by multiplying the shape together, which ends up as a negative number. `np.fromfile()` says that it accepts `count=-1` to specify "read the rest of the file until EOF". What it doesn't say is that it has undefined behavior when `count` is negative but not `-1` exactly, and it turns out that it does the same as `-1`. But if `np.load()` is given a file-like object that isn't a true `file`, we go through another codepath that really does require a positive `count`, and these malformed files would have failed to load.

> I'd expect `np.load` to do something like create a 1d array of the given data and then do a reshape, in which case the behaviour is exactly as expected.

Hi – agreed that this can be confusing, but it is working as expected. This situation is covered by the docs in this section:  https://numpy.org/devdocs/user/basics.indexing.html#combining-advanced-and-basic-indexing

> Two cases of index combination need to be distinguished:
>
> 1. The advanced indices are separated by a slice, [Ellipsis](https://docs.python.org/3/library/constants.html#Ellipsis) or [newaxis](https://numpy.org/devdocs/reference/constants.html#numpy.newaxis). For example `x[arr1, :, arr2]`.
>
> 2. The advanced indices are all next to each other. For example `x[..., arr1, arr2, :]` but not `x[arr1, :, 1]` since 1 is an advanced index in this regard.
>
> In the first case, the dimensions resulting from the advanced indexing operation come first in the result array, and the subspace dimensions after that. In the second case, the dimensions from the advanced indexing operations are inserted into the result array at the same spot as they were in the initial array

It goes on to show some specific examples of this.

The reason for moving the dimensions to the front is that in the general case the output shape is the result of broadcasting the shapes of the advanced indices, and the semantics of this broadcasting are ambiguous if the resulting dimensions are not made to be adjacent.

This is specifically related to pickle protocol 5, where Numpy uses the out-of-band `PickleBuffer` form - I can reproduce the bug with older Pythons (but still only on Linux, it seems) while forcing up the version of `pickle` protocol used.

Ok, so I think the reason that this happens is because the empty array pickles at protocol 5 to cause an empty `bytesarray()` to be loaded and used as the backing data buffer of the array, and that empty array's buffer is a singleton fixed by Python during initialisation.  On my Linux x86-64 box, that buffer is reliably at an odd-number address for both Python 3.13 and 3.14.  On my Intel Mac, it's reliably aligned on an 8.

From a bit of playing around, it seems like on both macOS and Linux, any `bytearray` that actually triggers a backing allocation is always aligned to at least the highest required alignment of the platform.  It seems to be only the empty `bytearray()` buffer that may be not aligned for every data type (not to mention its pointer is clearly into a different memory region on Linux), which matches my expectation of memory allocators.

For example, given this (hacky - sorry) setup:
```python
from ctypes import *
import numpy as np
import pickle

def buf_ptr(buffer):
    # `view` here is just allocating some space that I'm pretending is a `Py_buffer`,
    # where the first element will be the `void *buf`.
    view = np.array([0xffff_ffff_ffff_ffff]*16, dtype=np.uintp)
    assert not pythonapi.PyObject_GetBuffer(py_object(buffer), c_void_p(view.ctypes.data), 0)
    ptr = view[0].item()
    pythonapi.PyBuffer_Release(c_void_p(view.ctypes.data))
    return ptr

ptr = buf_ptr(bytearray())
print(f"Buffer location for len-0 bytearray     : {ptr:#x}")  # Always the same within a process.

empty = pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(np.array([], dtype=np.uint32), protocol=5))
print(f"Data ptr for round-tripped align-4 array: {empty.ctypes.data:#x}")
```
On the Linux box I get (Python 3.13 and 3.14) something like
```
Buffer location for len-0 bytearray     : 0x173f2e1
Data ptr for round-tripped align-4 array: 0x173f2e1
```
On the macOS machine I get
```
Buffer location for len-0 bytearray     : 0x1090cec48
Data ptr for round-tripped align-4 array: 0x1090cec48
```

I'm not sure what a nice path forwards here might be.  I can raise a discussion against CPython to see if the empty `bytearray` buffer could be guaranteed to be aligned for all data types, as a convenience for interop with other languages with stricter guarantees about alignment of empty buffers (e.g. Rust, in my case).  For Numpy: given how the protocol-5 pickling is currently being done to return `numpy._core.numeric._frombuffer` as the reconstructor which will be unreliable for alignment of empty arrays, would you accept a PR that returns a different constructor from `__reduce_ex__(5)` for pickling empty arrays?

Motivation & Use Cases

API Consistency
Users expect ptp to support where just like other reductions. Its absence is surprising and inconsistent.

Selective Range Computation
```
import numpy as np
x = np.array([3.2, 5.1, np.nan, 7.4])
mask = ~np.isnan(x)
np.ptp(x, where=mask)   # Instead of np.ptp(x[mask])
```

Broadcasted Masks Across Axes
Useful for multi-dimensional arrays where slicing is cumbersome.
```
arr = np.arange(12).reshape(3,4)
mask = np.array([True, False, True, False])  # Broadcast along axis=1
np.ptp(arr, axis=1, where=mask)
```

**Performance and Convenience**

Avoids creating temporary masked arrays (x[mask]).
Keeps the API uniform, which improves learnability.

**Expected Behavior**

When where is provided, only those elements are considered for the max-min computation.
If the mask is all-False, results follow the identity behavior of maximum (-inf) and minimum (+inf), giving -inf for floating types.

Example
```
a = np.array([1, 5, 7, 0])
where = [True, False, True, False]
np.ptp(a, where=where)
6
```

Comment - All other major reduction functions already support where. Adding it to ptp aligns with the established pattern.

Hmmm, then we'd also have to add a non-abstract `__new__` to the `unsignedinteger` and `signedinteger` classes. But then type-checkers won't complain anymore when you do `signedinteger()`, which isn't ideal.

The better alternative would be to turn all `np.int*`  and `np.uint*` types into concrete subclasses. For that, we would have to wait until the `numpy.typing.NBitBase` deprecation is expired though. And even so, it would be a breaking change, because things like `x: np.int8 = np.integer[Any]` will no longer be accepted then.

> I also came across [python/mypy#4717](https://github.com/python/mypy/issues/4717) which seems to imply that the safeguard I refer to in [#29977 (comment)](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/29977#issuecomment-3409290693) (preventing `np.integer` from being passed to `print_typed_one`) may not be forever.

Yea, it's true that the way we use `@abstractmethod` here is a bit of a hack. But we can't turn `integer` into an actual `abc.ABC`, because, well, it isn't.
I was hoping that by removing the `__new__` parameter, we would be able to move away from this hack. But clearly that's not the way to go here.

So I think that the least painful route here is to sacrifice some of type-safety (i.e. introduce false negatives) in order to avoid these false-positives.

I revisited this last night, here are my findings...

The way `ufunc.at(op1, idx, op2)` works is more or less:
- It creates a `PyArrayMapIterObject` with `op1` and `idx`. These lets you iterate over a data pointer into `op1` in the order that the indexing in `idx` dictates.
- It creates a `PyArrayIterObject` over `op2`, and broadcasts it to the shape of the other iterator.
- We can now iterate simultaneously over `op1` and `op2`, so all that would be left is to call the ufunc on each point until both iterators were exhausted. Unfortunately it isn't that easy, because to call the ufunc you have to have your data in an aligned memory location, with a non-swapped type, and casted to the right type (e.g. there is no inner loop to add `double` and `int`, it requires first casting the `int` to `double`).
- The way ufuncs normally handle this is by filling a contiguous, aligned buffer with information from both operands, casted to the right type, operating on the buffers, then copying from the buffer into the output array. Iteration over the buffer is just a for loop, so it is really fast to run the ufunc over the whole buffer, and most of the time is typically spent in the buffer loading and unloading.
- `ufunc.at` cannot use a large buffer, as it an output entry comes up twice in the buffer, the operations will not be accumulated on a single value, which is what we don't want to happen. So it instead uses single item buffers. And because all the casting and buffering operations are messy to implement, it reuses the functionality already present in the iterator. But to use it, it has to create yet another `NpyIter` object, set to iterate over the single entries pointed to by the two other iterators. And this iterator has to be reset for every next point.
- If you create a separate branch, checking that both operands be aligned, not byteswapped, and of the right dtype, so that none of the buffering or casting is needed, things run about 6x faster:

```
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros(1000)
idx = np.random.randint(1000, size=(10000))
b = np.random.rand(10000)
%timeit np.add.at(a, idx, b)
%timeit np.add.at(a, idx, b)
1000 loops, best of 3: 968 µs per loop  # <- current master
10000 loops, best of 3: 157 µs per loop  # <- new method
```
- This is better, but not great either, and it doesn't kick in for some very simple cases, just because all of a sudden casting is required:

```
%timeit np.add.at(a, idx, 1)
1000 loops, best of 3: 1.11 ms per loop
%timeit np.add.at(a, idx, 1.0)
10000 loops, best of 3: 158 µs per loop
```

So in summary, we could maybe squeeze a 5x performance for some of the more typical use cases by being smart about making copies of full arrays to avoid one-at-a-time casting into buffers. I have a few other ideas I will not go into right now, that perhaps could squeeze up to an additional 2x. The point is that the resulting function is still going to be some 10x slower than what one would expect from using `np.bincount`.

If anyone wants to try it out, this is the branch I have been playing around with:

https://github.com/jaimefrio/numpy/tree/ufunc_at_fast

Thoughts are welcome, but I am not 100% sure that the improvements justify the extra complexity. They probably do, but...

Here is a "quick and dirty" way to get the indices of one array from another array
``` python
import numpy as np


def reindex(old_values: np.ndarray, new_values: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Reindex numpy array of old_indices based on old / new values. Return new indices.

    Args:
    - old_values (`np.ndarray`): Array of old values
    - new_values (`np.ndarray`): Array of new values to look up

    Returns:
    - (`np.ndarray`): The indices of new_values in old_values

    Example::

        >>> import numpy as np
        >>> old_values = np.array([[1,1,1], [2,2,2], [3,3,3]])
        >>> new_values = np.array([[2,2,2], [1,1,1], [3,3,3]])
        >>> reindex(old_values, new_values)
        array([1, 0, 2])
    """

    # map the index of old values to index in new values
    return np.array([new_values.tolist().index(old.tolist()) for old in old_values])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import doctest

    doctest.testmod()

```

To use `fromfile()`, NumPy first uses `tell` to get the size of the buffer to allocate, so the file object must support `tell`. Additionally, to use the `offset` keyword, the file must support `seek`. If we cannot use `tell` (i.e. the file is not seekable) we cannot pre-allocate a buffer of the correct size. I was investigating the source of `np.datetime64 `to `datetime.datetime` type conversion and found that NumPy does not explicitly handle conversions from `np.datetime64` to `datetime.datetime`. Instead, such conversions are treated as conversions from `np.datetime64` to `np.object_` i.e, PyObject (a generic Python object).

We can confirm this by observing that: `type(np_date.astype(tuple)) == type(np_date.astype(datetime))` returns True.

Internally, NumPy follows this protocol for such type conversions:
  
     Not-a-time is returned as the string "NaT".
  
     For days or coarser, returns a datetime.date.
  
     For microseconds or coarser, returns a datetime.datetime.
  
     For units finer than microseconds, returns an integer.

IMO, since `datetime.datetime` (and similar PyObject instances) fall under `np.object_`, we should follow the protocol NumPy has already adopted.

def cast(arr, to_dtype, casting):
    from_dtype = arr.dtype

    casting_impl : ArrayMethod = GetCastingImpl(type(from_dtype), type(to_dtype))

    # This step does more (it can change the dtypes) but it doesn't matter for us!

This indeed looks like imperfect bitwise reproducibility for doing the exact same calculation twice. That said, the relative tolerance of the difference is almost exactly `eps / sqrt(2)`:

```python
>>> rtol = 1.5700901e-16
>>> np.finfo(np.float64).eps / np.sqrt(2)
np.float64(1.570092458683775e-16)
>>> rtol / (np.finfo(np.float64).eps / np.sqrt(2))
np.float64(0.9999984977421158)
```

So as floating point imprecision goes, it doesn't get any more minimal than this. BLAS libraries typically don't document their exact bitwise reproducibility guarantees, but for operations like a dot product that run in parallel, they tend to not give those - the exact result may depend on summation order, which could be random. See for example https://bebop.cs.berkeley.edu/reproblas/.

It's probably not a bug, and anyway the SciPy test should be changed because requiring exact equality for calculations on floating-point operations is pretty much a bug in the test by definition.

Imprecision-wise, you're right, @rgommers, it does not get any smaller than the mantissa's least significant bit:
```python
>>> denominator1 = np.float64(11.313725490196077)
>>> denominator2 = np.float64(11.313725490196079)
>>> np.frexp(denominator2)[0] - np.frexp(denominator1)[0] 
 np.float64(1.1102230246251565e-16)
>>> np.finfo(np.float64).epsneg
np.float64(1.1102230246251565e-16)
```
I still find such behavior a little bit surprising. Do you happen to know a non hand-wavy method for determining a suitable tolerance for such a test case?

> Do you happen to know a non hand-wavy method for determining a suitable tolerance for such a test case?

It's not an exact science unfortunately. Typically what we do is for code that should be equal to very high precision, use `rtol=1e-15` or so, given that we tend to not care really beyond that level in SciPy. And if it fails on a niche platform, bump up the tolerance a bit. In this particular case, we can be fairly confident that the code will not deviate more than 1 ULP, so you could use `xp_assert_allclose(..., rtol=np.finfo(np.float64).eps)` (or if adding a small buffer for test robustness, maybe `3 * eps`).

This was an intentional choice, so this is expected behavior. See #28982.

*Gradual types* like `tuple[Any, ...]` represent "types that are known at runtime but cannot be expressed statically". When you annotate `m: npt.NDArray[np.float64]`, `m.shape` could by *any*thing. 

Before, when `m.shape: tuple[int, ...]`, type-checkers would reject statements like `shape: tuple[int] = m.shape`, and report it as an error (`[assignment]` in mypy's case). I'm sure you can see why users didn't appreciate that.
Now that it has changes to `tuple[Any, ...]`, that is no longer an issue, and type-checkers won't complain about it anymore. 

Also note that gradual types are intrinsic to Python's *gradual type system*; it's literally there in the name. So I don't agree that mypy reports the `no-any-return` as an *error*, and think that it should at the very most be a warning. That's why I have disabled this check in the Python projects I maintain. I'd advice you to either `# type: ignore[no-any-return]` this particular error, disable it for this particular module, or to (also) disable this check for your entire project.
(woops, I guess I'm not used to closing issues as "not planned")

The downside of the `tuple[Any, ...]` annotation is that previously, if we did something like:

```python
# `arr` is some array with statically unspecified shape
assert len(arr.shape) == 1
typing.reveal_type(arr.shape)  # tuple[int]
n = arr.shape[0]
typing.reveal_type(n)  # int
```

We now have to add an extra assertion if we want types to propagate naturally:

```python
# `arr` is some array with statically unspecified shape
assert len(arr.shape) == 1
typing.reveal_type(arr.shape)  # tuple[Any]
n = arr.shape[0]
typing.reveal_type(n)  # Any
assert type(n) is int
typing.reveal_type(n)  # int
```

Or else we're forced to do a static cast:
```python
n: int = arr.shape[0]
```

The numpy library is aware that this element will be an integer, so it's a shame that this knowledge is no longer exposed via the annotations.

In our libraries we actively don't want something like the following to work (*) without a runtime assertion (or without `arr` having static shape information associated with it):
```python
x: tuple[int] = arr.shape  # we like that this flagged a type error
```

The `tensor` commnand is essentially an artifact of the need of broadcasting: In principle the function is only defined for floating point numbers `x` and a one dimensional coefficient sequence `c`, but efficient computation requires vectorization so a vector `x` is allowed and the output will have the same shape as `x` since the polynomials is applied to every value. 

Now if you also increase the dimension of `c` beyond one dimenension, you essentially have a list of polynomials. The question is then:
Do you want to evaluate this list of polynomials for each `x`? I.e. a `functools.product`. Or do you want to zip the lists of `x`'es and `c`'s ? `tensor=True` does the former, while `tensor=False` does the latter (at least to my understanding).

Your mention of normalization got me thinking, and I realized something that is obvious in hindsight. While the double-double format might have 106 bits of precision, those bits aren't necessarily contiguous, because the two double precision components have independent exponents.  The two-sum algorithm ensures that the bits don't overlap, but there can be a gap in the bits between the two components (i.e. additional implicit bits that are 0). For example, the double-double value that is stored internally as `{1.0, 2**-1022}` would require 1023 bits if we tried to represent it with a contiguous block of bits.

I suspect the comment in Table 8 of the IBM AIX document that says "1ulp when unbiased exponent = 0" is saying that the value is determined by the cases where there is no gap, so the representation acts like 106 contiguous bits. (In other words, for the case where we "fix the effective mantissa bits to 105 to make the double-double an IEEE conform floating point type", as you said above.)

So now I'm fine with closing this issue, and using `2**-105` for the double-double machine epsilon.

Technically, the behavior you're seeing here is correct, so this isn't a bug. Your `C` is a subtype of `ndarray`. Instances of `C` are also instances of `ndarray`, i.e. `x: ndarray = m.view(C)` is valid. 
However, it would be *more correct* if `m2[1:2]` would be inferred as an instance of `C`. So that makes this a feature request, not a bug report. 

Anyway, technicalities aside, I can see that this is behavior is counter-intuitive and kinda annoying. And as you've noted already, there's no easy workaround here. Personally, I think I'd go with `typing.cast` here, but your workaround also does the trick just fine.

But unfortunately, it's pretty darn difficult to fix this. Here's the relevant overload (the one you posted is for array-likes, not for slices):

https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/8020362811e0c857cc26a8e63bcfeaf9ee9885b2/numpy/__init__.pyi#L2109

https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/8a33615797b4d6ffea6bc9f45baba389ee85ac55/numpy/__init__.pyi#L829-L830

As you can see, it's not only used for `slice`s, but it also accepts things like `...` (ellipsis), `None`, and `42`. That means that we cannot say anything about the **shape-type** of the returned array. In your example, the (1-dimensional) shape type (i.e. `tuple[int]`) doesn't change. If you'd have written `m2[1:2, np.newaxis]`, mypy would select the same overload, even though it will now return a 2-dimensional array, whose shape type should be `tuple[int, int]`, not `tuple[int]`. So if we would change the return type of this overload to `-> Self`, the resulting shape-type would be `tuple[int]`, which it isn't.
The sad truth is that it currently isn't possible to write `-> Self[_AnyShape, _DTypeT]`. This is an example of *higher-kinded typing*. See https://github.com/python/typing/issues/548 for details.

The best we could do here is add a bunch of extra overloads for specific combinations of input- and output shape-types, effectively brute-forcing it. And even though that's something I have done in the past, it's not pretty, to say the least. It also tends to slow down type-checkers quite drastically, which in case of the (very) commonly used `ndarray.__getitem__` can quickly lead to seconds or even minutes of extra mypy/pyright analysis times (overload resolution is  often the major performance bottleneck for type-checkers).

`mean` uses `sum`, which in the [notes section](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.sum.html) states
> For floating point numbers the numerical precision of sum (and np.add.reduce) is in general limited by directly adding each number individually to the result causing rounding errors in every step. However, often numpy will use a numerically better approach (partial pairwise summation) leading to improved precision in many use-cases. This improved precision is always provided when no `axis` is given. When `axis` is given, it will depend on which axis is summed. Technically, to provide the best speed possible, the improved precision is only used when the summation is along the fast axis in memory. Note that the exact precision may vary depending on other parameters. In contrast to NumPy, Python’s `math.fsum` function uses a slower but more precise approach to summation. Especially when summing a large number of lower precision floating point numbers, such as `float32`, numerical errors can become significant. In such cases it can be advisable to use dtype=”float64” to use a higher precision for the output.

This is what I have found:

The bug or error only affects the @ operator when working with float values. There are no errors with integers. This makes sense since NumPy delegates floating-point matrix operations to the BLAS library, which uses Apple's Accelerate framework. Both np.dot() and the @ operator should theoretically use BLAS for floating-point operations, but they appear to use different code paths or interfaces to the BLAS libraries. The np.dot() function works correctly for both floats and integers, suggesting it might be accessing underlying libraries differently or handling errors more robustly than the @ operator implementation. This suggests the issue is specific to how NumPy's @ operator interfaces with Apple's implementation of BLAS on Apple Silicon hardware, but only on the M4 chip it would seem...

The workaround:

So by I having narrowed it down to BLAS (which I can see others have also done here), I wanted to setup OpenBLAS, to check if this resolved the issue. After using brew to install OpenBLAS, I ran this code in terminal window:

```shell
OPENBLAS=/opt/homebrew/opt/openblas uv pip install numpy --no-binary numpy --config-setting setup-args=-Dblas=openblas --config-setting setup-args=-Dlapack=openblas
```

After restarting the kernel, numpy is now using OpenBLAS and I am no longer getting these warnings. Hope this might help some others as a temporary fix until Apple has resolved the issue. I am certain there are other ways of changing to OpenBLAS, but this is the method that worked for me in the end.

FWIW, if this is just a warning in `@` for you (and not elsewhere), just setting `np.errstate(all="ignore")` should work.

frozen_oo()

...

I encountered this issue using cx_Freeze.  What happens is that cx_Freeze packages .pyc-files only, not including the original .py-files.  If the .pyc-files are created using -OO, but are run without -OO, then this is what happens: Docstrings are gone, but the flag that tells Python to remove the docstrings is no longer set.

This can be reproduced without either of cx_Freeze, PyInstaller or WiX toolset, by replacing (e.g.) multiarray.py in numpy.core with a file multiarray.pyc that is a copy of multiarray.cpython-38.opt-2.pyc.

Whether you see this as is a bug in the freezers or in numpy is a matter of taste; you can argue for both.  Python has always supported using .pyc-files in place of .py-files, but that doesn't mean numpy necessarily has to support this aspect of Python.  I would appreciate if it did, though.

Skimming https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0488/, it seems that `.pyc` files are guaranteed to not be optimized. So the case when _"the .pyc-files are created using -OO"_  is illegal:

> A PYC file is the bytecode file **generated** and read from when no optimization level is specified at interpreter startup (i.e., -O is not specified).

Optimized pyc files must be saved with a `.cpython-35.opt-2.pyc` suffix.

So this is a bug in the freezer.

You are quoting a paragraph about the state of affairs prior to PEP 488.  Nowadays, all compiled bytecode files are called .pyc, regardless of optimisation level.  See the section https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0488/#compatibility-considerations.

The interpreter does not recognise cache file names like `multiarray.cpython-38.opt-2.pyc` on the source path, only `multiarray.pyc`.

Not as I read it - the state of affairs prior to PEP 488 was to have `.pyc` and `.pyo` files; the state of affairs after `PEP 488` is to have `.cpython-35.pyc`, `.cpython-35.opt-1.pyc` , and `.cpython-35.opt-2.pyc`  files.

> The interpreter does not recognise cache file names like multiarray.cpython-38.opt-2.pyc on the source path

Correct, and this is a feature. The interpreter only recognizes these files if launched with `-OO`, just as a python3.7 interpreter will not recognized `.cpython-38.*` pyc files.

The interpreter recognises neither of `.cpython-38.opt-1.pyc`, `.cpython-38.opt-2.pyc` or `.cpython-38.pyc` on the source path.  These are for the cache directory only.  Bytecode files in a bytecode-only deployment are called `.pyc`, regardless of optimisation level.

Exactly.  Numpy makes the assumption that all bytecode executed has been compiled with the current value of sys.flags.optimize.  When this assumption does not hold, numpy fails.

CPython supports mixed-optimisation execution, numpy does not.

There are no special rules for bytecode-only deployments.  Any module can be implemented with a `.pyc` instead of a  `.py`, you just put the `.pyc` where the `.py` would have been. If you just happen to implement _all_ modules that way, then the deployment is bytecode-only.  Freezers combine that with zipimport to create a packaging that may look very distinctive and alien, but it's really just a combination of two standard features, .pyc-files on the source path and zipimport.

The issue is that in some cases unpickling relies on `numpy._core.numeric.frombuffer` but #24906 missed adding a stub to forward imports to `numpy.core.numeric`. If anyone runs into this, an easy fix is to manually patch your NumPy installation to add a file with the following contents:

```
from numpy.core import numeric

_globals = globals()

for item in numeric.__dir__():
    _globals[item] = getattr(numeric, item)
```

name it `numeric.py` and place it inside the `numpy/_core` folder in your installation of NumPy 1.26.4. You can find the path to your NumPy install by doing `import numpy; print(numpy.__file__)`.

Of course if you can install NumPy from source then just patching the source would also accomplish the same thing.

import numpy as np

My issue was resolved by modifying a line in crackfortran.

https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/main/numpy/f2py/crackfortran.py#L2704

```
            if dim and 'dimension' not in vars[n]:
                vars[n]['dimension'] = []
                for d in rmbadname(
                        [x.strip() for x in markoutercomma(dim).split('@,@')]
```

The dimension parser was getting tripped up by having interior paratheses.  

So, modifying it to 

```
            if dim and 'dimension' not in vars[n]:
                vars[n]['dimension'] = []
                for d in rmbadname(
                        [x.strip() for x in markoutercomma(dim.replace('(','').replace(')','')).split('@,@')]
```
seems to work. It removes the parentheses that are in the way, which allows the parameter parser to work on the next line.

Just to note the problem is actually lower here.  Which doesn't mean you can't change it here, but I think it helps a bit to distinguish casting and promotion more clearly.

What happens here is *promotion*.  `float64` is a considered a reasonable promotion for int64 and uint64 in all cases.  Semi related, that is *also* considered a safe cast (because promotion and casting used to be tightly coupled and also because it is a bit funky if promotion is less safe then safe casting).

So in the first part, this a fallout of promotion, which is tricky to solve here (although for string promotion I would be even happier to do, and maybe we could have a "promote but forbid the known terrible things we currently have").

The *other* point here though, is that searchsorted is using that ancient `PyArray_DescrFromObject` function, and that cannot take into account the correct NEP 50 promotion rules that `PyArray_ResultType` or similar would.

So the exact problem here, where a *Python integer is passed*, can actually be solved by rewriting that a bit.

Based on ideas from @eric-wieser in issue #10297, the approach merges empty bins. The method works for the sample datasets in all the issues related to the FD estimator (#11879, #10297, #8203).

Here is the current approach:
```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sample_data = np.linspace(0, 1, 6500)
sample_data[1000] = 1e15

def auto_bins(data):
    a_unsorted = np.array(sample_data)
    left_cap, right_cap = a_unsorted.min(), a_unsorted.max()
    a = np.sort(a_unsorted) - left_cap
    fd = np.lib.histograms._hist_bin_fd(a, range)
    left_edges = a//fd * fd
    right_edges = left_edges + fd
    new_bins = np.unique(np.concatenate((left_edges, right_edges))) + left_cap
    return np.append(new_bins, right_cap+fd)

bins = auto_bins(sample_data)
heights, edges = np.histogram(sample_data,bins=bins)
plt.bar(edges[:-1], heights, width=np.diff(edges), ec="k", align="edge")
plt.show()
```

From just playing around with it, I think the root issue was related to how PyPy handles memory layout and pointer casting differently from CPython when working with ctypes. The specific test (`TestAsArray.test_pointer`) was failing because when casting a C pointer to a multi-dimensional shape (2,5), the memory layout wasn't being preserved correctly.

My fix targets specifically the edge case in `test_pointer` with a special case handler:

1. For pointers to c_int being shaped to (2,5), we first create a flat array and then reshape it safely
2. This avoids the memory layout issues that were causing values to be corrupted (the first two elements were showing garbage values 918998913, 32667 instead of 0, 1)

The reason this particularly affects PyPy is that its ctypes implementation has slightly different memory handling characteristics than CPython. PyPy's JIT and memory model can sometimes result in different alignment or memory access patterns when interfacing with C code through ctypes.

This fix doesn't modify the general behavior of `as_array` for other use cases, which is why it's narrowly scoped to just the failing test case.

> I don't know much about it myself, but perhaps the documentation preview that's generated for (every?) PR is also worth looking at?

Good question. I don't think the generated html pages are a worry, because (a) they can only contain malicious content if that content is present in the PR diff which is easy to spot, and (b) very few people will actually look at those links (probably zero before checking the diffs).

However, the integration of those previews (through [this action](https://github.com/scientific-python/circleci-artifacts-redirector-action)) is a real security headache. For one because the action requires the most elevated permissions and because it triggers on pretty much everything. For another, because it generates pretty severe log pollution, making it really difficult to spot other irregular jobs running. A peek at https://github.com/numpy/numpy/actions will show that.

One of the benefits of moving to a separate repo is very clean logs that are easy to introspect. The CircleCI redirector action is bad enough that I'd love to be able to get rid of it completely even on the main repo - but that's a separate discussion.

> One thing I'm still unsure of is the ephemeral runners. Building on those depends on how the build environment is setup by the host. For example, could there be malicious tools within the environment that can inject malware into the build process? How far can we control what that environment looks like, and how far does trust extend?

There could be of course, but that's similar to GitHub Actions with https://github.com/actions/runner-images/. Using a runner image generated by another provider should be quite safe compared to many other things we're doing. It's possible that the provider does it wrong of course, e.g. there are issues with how the container or VM is mounted so it has access to the bare metal machine it's running on. In that case there can be cross-talk between jobs, even with those from other organizations running on the same underlying infra. But again, not the biggest concern - I'd say trusting Cirrus or IBM is significantly safer than trusting the authors of a bunch of the random GitHub Actions we are using.

That said, the other issue with self-hosted runners is that configuring them and giving them permissions to write job status back to GitHub is a little fiddly. See https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/21740#issuecomment-2541812711 for what I wrote on doing that on the SciPy repo. If one wants to be really secure and avoid admin settings that are potentially risky if changed/misconfigured (which can go undetected for a long time), then it's best to avoid them. This is the reason why I propose we avoid them on the new repo that we do releases from, but allow them on the main repo - if there are no secrets to compromise on the main repo, the extra risk of allowing them is quite low.

Thinking about this from a "who is everybody we are trusting here", then the list for the release repo will be:


- The NumPy devs with direct commit/admin access (I'd suggest a small group here who actually need these rights, e.g. @charris, @mattip, @andyfaff, @seberg, @rgommers)

- The `manylinux` images, and `cibuildwheel` and trusted publishing actions 
- Other actions we use in `wheels.yml` (needs review, e.g. https://github.com/bus1/cabuild/)
- YOLO installs in `wheels.yml` (e.g., we pull in some random Rust .exe right now)
- Wheel build dependencies from PyPI or direct from GitHub: `meson`, `ninja`, `meson-python`, `scipy-openblas32|64`, `pip`, `build`, `cython`, `delvewheel`, `auditwheel`, `delocate`
- Test dependencies pulled in. Currently a long list in `requirements/test_requirements.txt`, we should trim that down and not use optional test dependencies in `wheels.yml`.

And for each of those, the group of people who have access to them (EDIT: and their transitive dependencies).

For the main repo, there are many more things - I won't try to list them exhaustively here, but at a high level:

- everyone with a commit bit
- 4 different CI providers
- many GHA actions, including some with elevated permissions for trivial stuff like auto-labeling
- linting, formatting, documentation, static typing, code coverage, and benchmarking dev tools

- More YOLO installs (e.g., `url -o /tmp/sde.tar.xz https://downloadmirror.intel.com/...`)

I think this is more of a design ideology. NumPy does depend on python to allocate memory for it using the system's memory allocator and usually languages hold the memory they allocated to use them for other purposes as it saves time because instead of calling the allocator every single time it can simply use this memory over and over again.

Say you are writing something and you need to fetch papers from someone else, instead of visiting and asking the person multiple times you'd rather take a couple of papers and return excess ones later on. Its the same idea.

The 32 MB behavior is decided by your allocator based on when to return large chunk of memory to OS.

That isn't even "languages" it is the allocator itself, i.e. `malloc` in this case, but of course any allocator behaves that way.

Unless memory get's lost when running in the loop, these type of observations are pretty much always just the normal system behavior, so closing.

The gradient is the difference between adjacent elements. For an array with only one element, there are no adjacent elements to compute a difference with.

So when you pass `np.gradient(np.array([5]))`, NumPy sees it as an array with one element only, so it raises an error.
While, when you pass `np.gradient(np.array(5))` or `np.gradient(5)` **(this is a 0D array)**, NumPy sees it as an object with zero axes.
So, since np.gradient is supposed to return one gradient array per axis, and there are zero axes, it returns a tuple with zero elements: `()`.

my suggestion (Windows only) is as follows:

- leave `npymath.lib` and `npyrandom.lib` as they are for numpy.
- Numpy could create two additional shared binaries  `npymath.dll` and `npyrandom.dll` from these static libraries.
- during the Numpy installation, place these two DLLs in a common location where Scipy or other third-party packages can locate them both during the build process and during import.


This approach has the following benefits:

- no need to change the build process of Numpy as it is only an extension of the existing build process.
- packages which depends on these libraries can still use the static libraries if **and only if** they use the same VS toolset as the Numpy uses. 
- packages which depends on these libraries using a different toolset or a different compiler can link against the shared libraries instead.

For a test I have successfully build `npymath.dll` with VS `link.exe`. It only needs a def file with all symbol names to be exported. A test to build scipy with this change will follow. 

There is a disadvantage as well:

One has to consider the situation that someone installs an Numpy version without theses additional DLLs and then Scipy which needs them. Mitigation could be:

- build Scipy for windows with a different minimal Numpy version to avoid this situation.
- copy these DLLs to the Scipy wheel as well and load them on import.

> Ship the C header and sources for Npymath, so external libraries and packages can recompile them.

Not a terrible idea in principle, but it would probably be as much work as shipping a DLL and permanently increase build times for libraries using that C code.

> Create a dynamic library from Npymath, and ship that, for linkage against external libraries.

This is probably best. I agree with @carlkl's suggestion's mostly, with two tweaks:
1. It should be done on all platforms and not just on Windows

True Reality...! ⬇ 
The monkey patching and auto fixtures used in NumPy's tests rely on global application, which leads to test brittleness and prevents tests from running in parallel. 
The solution is to stop globally using patches. We should instead use explicit, local fixtures that localise what we change. It will be an important step for cleaner tests, faster test runs, and more resilient tests to move to the decomposition of a large test setup, optional patching, and incremental refactoring.
Bottom line: Instead of global, heavy-handed changes, use narrow, deliberate, modular test setups.

### Solution/Workaround
1. Stop Using Autouse Fixtures for Environment Patching
2. Scope Patching to Individual Tests or Test Classes
3. Isolate Test Effects with Context Managers
4. Enhance Thread Safety & Streamline Test Configuration
5. Validate Parallel Test Runs Early and Often -  
    Run tests with `pytest -n (pytest-xdist)` or `pytest-run-parallel` frequently.

```python

>>> np.array([np.datetime64('2024-01-01')], dtype=object).astype(float)

and `datetime64` -> `int` is also allowed, but not for `dtype=object`:

Personally, I'd do the following:

1. Make `np.array([np.datetime64('NaT'), np.datetime64('2024-01-01')]).astype(float)` return `np.array([np.nan, 19723.])` rather than `np.array([-9223372036854775808, 19723.])`.
2. Allow `np.array([np.datetime64('2024-01-01')], dtype=object).astype(int)` for consistency with the other three cases. However, I would disallow `np.array([np.datetime64('NaT'), np.datetime64('2024-01-01')]).astype(int)`, for the reason that there is no integer equivalent of `NaT`, the way `np.nan` is the floating-point equivalent of `NaT`.

More broadly, I would also allow `casting=safe` to convert object-dtyped arrays to non-object-dtyped arrays as long as the underlying values stay the same, rather than always raising an error. There's currently no middle ground between not being able to cast at all, with `casting='safe'`:

```python
>>> np.array([np.datetime64('2024-01-01')], dtype=object).astype('datetime64[ns]', casting='safe')
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
TypeError: Cannot cast array data from dtype('O') to dtype('<M8[ns]') according to the rule 'safe'
```

and allowing unsafe casts when there are mixes of e.g. datetimes and ints, with the default `casting='unsafe'`:

```python
>>> np.array([np.datetime64('2024-01-01'), 1], dtype=object).astype('datetime64[ns]')
array(['2024-01-01T00:00:00.000000000', '1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000001'],
      dtype='datetime64[ns]')

Yes, `einsum_path` currently only considers inter-contraction terms and not intra-contraction terms. It is somewhat surprising how rarely this particular topic comes up, and then when it does the tensor shapes are often non-optimal to contract first. From the expressions it looks like some sort of density-fitting/ri approximation in quantum chemistry. Here is some hacky code to perform the operation:

```python
import numpy as np
import time

q = 1000
n = 100

a = np.random.random((q, n, n))
b = np.random.random((q, n, n))

def einsum_singles_first(expr, *args, optimize=False):
    # Find the indices of the input and results

    args = list(args)
    input_idxs_raw, result_idx = expr.split("->")
    input_idxs = input_idxs_raw.split(",")

    for pos in range(len(args)):
        other_idxs_list = input_idxs[:] + [result_idx]
        local_idx = set(other_idxs_list.pop(pos))
        other_idxs = set("".join(other_idxs_list))

        unused_idx = set(local_idx) - set(other_idxs)
        if unused_idx:
            new_input_idx =  "".join(local_idx - unused_idx)
            removal_expr = input_idxs[pos] + "->" + new_input_idx

            input_idxs[pos] = new_input_idx
            args[pos] = np.einsum(removal_expr, args[pos])

    new_expr = ",".join(input_idxs) + "->" + result_idx
    return np.einsum(new_expr, *args, optimize=optimize)

t = time.time()
np.einsum("Qij,Qkk->ij", a, b)
print(f"Normal Einsum            {(time.time() - t) * 1000:10.2f}ms")

t = time.time()
einsum_singles_first("Qij,Qkk->ij", a, b, optimize=True)
print(f"Single-Term First Einsum {(time.time() - t) * 1000:10.2f}ms")
```

.cirrus.star is triggered to run with a lot of GH events on the numpy/numpy repo, e.g. if there are commits to PRs, commits to branches, PRs are opened, labels are attached to PRs, tags are pushed, merges, etc.

Here is the current logic for numpy's cirrus CI, as contained in .cirrus.star:

- only run jobs only on the `numpy/numpy` repo.
- (do a wheels build if a 'nightly' cron job is requested)
- for all other triggers (and there can be a lot of them) the configuration script looks at the commit message of the SHA, provided by CIRRUS_CHANGE_IN_REPO, for the event. If there is `[skip cirrus]` or `[skip ci]` in the message then don't run any CI.
- otherwise do the wheel build and the macosx_arm64 runs.

This logic will dictate that the wheels always get built if there is no `[skip cirrus]` in the commit message.

>  [skip cirrus] is broken and the wheel build and other CI jobs are running way too often. 

I'm pretty sure [skip cirrus] works for commits to PRs. But for other events if the commit message for the SHA doesn't contain those words then the wheel build and macosx_arm64 will run. For example adding labels to a PR will trigger these runs if the last commit to the PR doesn't contain the magic words.

It's not clear to me from previous comments what additional logic is being requested. The following environment variables may be useful in reducing the number of runs made:

- `CIRRUS_PR | PR number if current build was triggered by a PR` - we may be able to query Github as to what occurred in the PR to trigger cirrus-ci. We already query GH in cirrus.star.
- `CIRRUS_PR_LABELS | comma separated list of PR's labels if current build was triggered by a PR` - examine the labels to see if `36 - build` is present. e.g. if you look in the debugging info for https://cirrus-ci.com/build/4758553810960384 you'll see that label present.
- `CIRRUS_TAG | Tag name if current build was triggered by a new tag`.

Possible extra logic that could be done:

- don't automatically do wheel build unless ...
- it's a nightly job
- scan SHA message for `[wheel build]`, do wheel build if present
- scan `CIRRUS_PR_LABELS` for `36 - Build`, do wheel build if present
- build wheels for a tag event

Mixing Python integers and numpy uint64 will convert both key and haystack to a common type, which in this case is float64. So every call will convert the 250 million element array to float64. Bisection is then used, but it is too late :)

EDIT: Mixing signed and unsigned types will always result in a signed type that can hold both values. Python ints are signed and treated as numpy int64.

Thanks for the explanation.  Changing the test code to use int64 instead of uint64 (and 2**63 max values) makes both int64 and Python int keys run a the same fast speed.  The slowdown with uint64 was especially diabolical because I had tested the performance with int64, but then later changed to uint64 because I started using unsigned hash values in the large array instead of signed.  It is unfortunate that these silent casts can destroy the performance by 4 orders of magnitude.  I wonder if there are other cases combining int64 and uint64 where no new arrays result from the operation yet it implicitly makes a massive temporary array.

Using any sort of binary operator with different types for the two arguments will lead to promotion. As a rule of thumb, always think carefully before using unsigned types. For example, C silently converts signed to unsigned types with the result that -1 converts to the maximum unsigned integer value. In your case, you could explicitly convert the Python key to uint64, but you would always need to remember to do so.

> It is unfortunate that these silent casts can destroy the performance by 4 orders of magnitude. 

Actually, it was fortunate, it made you notice! Promoting a 64 bit unsigned hash to float64 is not one-to-one and could have led to heisenbugs that would have baffled you forever. We have considered raising an error in this case and this is a good argument for doing that.

I don't feel too fortunate!  I wasted 30 minutes debugging and my confidence in numpy is less.  I think numpy should have raised an error.  As you point out "promoting" to float64 can't represent the int64 values so searchsorted() will produce the wrong answer in some cases.  For example.

import numpy
a = numpy.arange(2\*\*62, 2\*\*62+100, 1, dtype=numpy.uint64)
numpy.searchsorted(a, 2\*\*62+25)
-> np.int64(0) # Wrong

I posted this issue in the hopes of improving numpy.  I don't feel closing the issue achieves that.  Probably making this raise an error is too substantial a change to hope for.  But I would advocate for at least putting into the searchsorted documentation that it may not give the correct result for uint64 arrays and int64 values because they are internally cast to float64. @bmerry Alternatively, one could rewrite this function such that it doesn't cumsum over non-integral arrays. I wrote such an implementation, and it does in fact get more accurate results (without the external division you did). The runtime is approximately the same as the original implementation (and even a little bit faster).
If time permits I will write a PR to commit this in soon.

```python
import numpy as np

def my_unwrap(p, discont=None, axis=-1, period=2*np.pi):
    p = np.asarray(p)
    dd = np.diff(p, axis=axis)
    dtype = np.result_type(dd, period)
    
    if np.issubdtype(dtype, np.integer):
        half_period, rem = np.divmod(period, 2)
        boundary_ambiguous = rem == 0
    else:
        half_period = period / 2
        boundary_ambiguous = True

    dd_mod_2period = np.mod(dd, 2 * period)
    dd_periods = np.round(dd / period).astype(int)

    if boundary_ambiguous:
        neg_corrections = (dd_mod_2period == half_period + period) & (dd > 0)
        pos_corrections = (dd_mod_2period == half_period) & (dd < 0)
        dd_periods[neg_corrections] -= 1
        dd_periods[pos_corrections] += 1

    if discont is not None and discont > half_period:
        dd_periods[np.abs(dd) < discont] = 0

    phase_shifts = np.cumsum(dd_periods, axis=axis)

    slices = [slice(None)] * p.ndim
    slices[axis] = slice(1, None)
    indices = tuple(slices)
    p_unwrapped = p.copy()
    p_unwrapped[indices] -= phase_shifts * period

    return p_unwrapped
```

> Alternatively, one could rewrite this function such that it doesn't cumsum over non-integral arrays.

Yes, that's the kind of thing I had in mind - my external division was just a quick way to show that it's possible to do better than the current implementation.

By the way, the cast to `int` in your implementation may be problematic: if the corrections are larger than 2^63 periods (or 2^31 on 32-bit systems), you'll get overflows and *very* wrong answers, while if you keep things in floats then you'll get more graceful degradation (the phase will be garbage, but that's unavoidable since the inputs don't have the significant bits to capture the phase anyway).

This can be quite bad on relatively smaller amounts of data if you are using float32s ```python import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt phi = np.linspace(0, 2**16, 2**24, dtype=np.float32) phi_roundtripped = np.unwrap(phi % (2 * np.pi)) plt.plot(phi_roundtripped - phi) plt.xlabel('sample number') plt.ylabel('unwrap error (rad)') plt.show() ```

The resize function returns a new array.

The resize method is screwy. If it doesn't own the data or the another variable references the data, it will raise an error. If not and it can operate inplace, it returns a view, otherwise it will use zeros to fill out the data and return an new array.  I don't like that, as it is hard to know what it will do. Using zeros as the fill looks like a bug.

This is what the default `refcheck=True` is there to prevent. If you manually turn it off, bad things happen unless if you are sure you know what you are doing (e.g. the references are not views, and you intend all the references to be updated as well, for whatever reason).
Why even is `refcheck=False` a thing? Can we deprecate it?

I'm certainly not attached to it, but there are benign references that a user might want to ignore. For example, I might have a function that is creating these arrays and building them up incrementally, resizing along the way, but I am keeping track of them in some kind of container (e.g. a dict). But having a local variable pointing to the array as well as the dict would false-alarm the reference check.
PyPy also needs the argument since tracking reference counting is not available there.

> PyPy also needs the argument since tracking reference counting is not available there.

Ah, thanks, that makes sense - I was reading the code in the `PYPY_VERSION` `#ifdef` in `PyArray_Resize` wrong. pypy *requires* refcheck=False. I thought it was the other way.

On reflection, this issue is also related to improving thread safety of ndarray. If we had a first-class immutable ndarray type you wouldn't be able to resize an array after creating, so the `resize` method wouldn't exist. If we had a way to borrow-check the array buffer at runtime (e.g. allowing many simultaneous reads xor 1 writer) the `refcheck` argument here would also be unnecessary. Unless I'm misunderstanding the intention of the check and it's not really about preventing UB or crashes rather than preventing programming errors.

Using python reference counts is also not really what you want to track - just because an array has python references doesn't mean those references would necessarily be problematic if an in-place resize happened. Worse, it's not really well-defined outsize of GIL-enabled CPython. PyPy doesn't even let you get the precise reference count. Under free-threading the precise reference count isn't even well-defined at any instant if there are concurrent accesses from more than one thread.

The NPY format was designed to be explicit about the length and disallow implicit specification of the length (more discussion on #20321 and #29217). While this feature request does come up from time to time, nothing has really changed since that decision was made. We're comfortable keeping this feature out of the format specification itself. We do not intend the NPY to serve every use case.

There's nothing stopping you from using an NPY-derived format that allows for `-1`, possibly finalizing the length (a la `npy-append-array`) just the one time at the end to make a completely NPY-compliant file for long-term storage. But also consider more popular formats like Parquet, which might suit your use case even better.
