The place to implement (if in numpy) this would be in `numpy.random.Generator`, not a separate function. An efficient implementation might be more straightforward in Cython than this pure Python.

We are very conservative about adding functionality to `Generator`, but this would be the kind of contribution that I would not dismiss out of hand (as distinct from, say, contributing another named continuous probability distribution, which we won't accept). There is a gap in the functionality of `Generator.choice()` that this would address, but we may still decide it's not worth the effort.

Unfortunately, given the current semantics of `Generator.choice(..., replace=False)` and the interpretation of the `shape=` argument in that case, I don't think that we can just add it to `choice()`. Probably, we'd need a separate method that implements random sampling from an array without replacement, with particular attention in the argument specification paid to the distinction between how many items are in each sample (what you called `sample_size`) and how many (in what shape) samples we want to draw (what you called `n_iterations`).

To me `Generator.choice` seems to be the most natural to add this. Creating a separate function for this seems unnecessary, when there is a need for an additional parameter anyway.

Changing the signature shouldn't be done lightly, but adding a new function isn't any less of a burden than adding an optional parameter to an existing function. Another possibility would be to allow something like `tuple(tuple(int), int)` where the outer int specifies n_iterations

The semantics of the proposed addition would be quite different from the current semantics, keyed by `replace=True` or `replace=False`. When you have a function that changes its semantics based on a boolean argument that you expect to be passed as a literal, it's a code smell that indicates that it should just be another function instead. There's no real need for economy here; the 2-method implementation is simpler to implement and easier to document (which usually also means that it's easier to learn).

(I have long attributed this principle to Guido van Rossum, but I can no longer find the primary source.)

Vectorized sampling without replacement is a useful feature that we should include in NumPy.  Requests for this feature come up on stackoverflow now and then; here are some that I could find:

* (2024) [efficiently draw random samples without replacement from an array in python](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/79295206/efficiently-draw-random-samples-without-replacement-from-an-array-in-python)
* (2022) [numpy multiple random choice](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/72076229/numpy-multiple-random-choice)
* (2020) [Multiple sequences of random numbers without replacement](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/62642372/multiple-sequences-of-random-numbers-without-replacement)
* (2018) [numpy take many samples with no replacement by row](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/53891169/numpy-take-many-samples-with-no-replacement-by-row)
* (2016) [generate a 2D array of numpy.random.choice without replacement](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/37012244/generate-a-2d-array-of-numpy-random-choice-without-replacement)
* (2016) [numpy choose without replacement along specific dimension](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/40002821/numpy-choose-without-replacement-along-specific-dimension)

As @rkern noted, whatever we implement, it should be either a new `Generator` method or a modification of an existing `Generator` method.

Back in 2018, in a mailing list thread, I proposed a new function called `select` that would provide this functionality:

https://mail.python.org/archives/list/numpy-discussion@python.org/message/WASHPMLJSDW5EAUCATI6FVALMZZ74CFY/

I have since moved the github gist for `select` to [`numerand`](https://github.com/WarrenWeckesser/numerand), a repo where I keep a few experiments related to generating random stuff.  The function is briefly described in the repo's `README.md` file in the section [Random selection of elements from a sequence](https://github.com/WarrenWeckesser/numerand/blob/main/README.md#random-selection-of-elements-from-a-sequence). (As noted in the code, that version of `select` was written just to have a working version of the API.  It is not an efficient implementation.)  I'll summarize and extend the proposed API here, so you don't have to read the links.  The parameters `nsample` and `size` of `select` correspond to `sample_size` and `n_iterations` of `random_choice_without_replacement` shown above.

First, some background notes:

* The process of sampling `m` elements without replacement from a sequence of length `n` should be interpreted as a multivariate distribution.  Each [random variate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_variate) is a 1-d array of length `m`.  `m` is a parameter of the distribution, just like, for example, `nsample` is a parameter of the [multivarate_hypergeometric](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/random/generated/numpy.random.Generator.multivariate_hypergeometric.html) distribution.
* For the existing multivariate distributions (i.e. `dirichlet`, `multinomial`, `multivariate_hypergeometric` and `multivariate_normal`), each variate is a 1-d array with some length `m`; the actual parameter that determines `m` depends on the distribution.  The `size` parameter gives the shape of the collection of variates to be generated. It does not include the dimension of the variates.  When `size` is an integer, e.g. `size=r`, the output has shape `(r, m)`. More generally, when `size` is a tuple of integers, e.g. `size=(p, q, r)`, the shape of the result is `size + (m,)`, e.g. `(p, q, r, m)`.  When `size` is None, a single variate (i.e. 1-d array with shape `(m,)`) is generated.

  E.g.

  ```
  In [39]: rng.multinomial(10, pvals=[0.7, 0.2, 0.1], size=None)  # Generate a single variate.
  Out[39]: array([6, 3, 1])
  
  In [40]: rng.multinomial(10, pvals=[0.7, 0.2, 0.1], size=5)     # Generate 5 variates.
  Out[40]: 
  array([[4, 4, 2],
         [5, 2, 3],
         [6, 2, 2],
         [6, 3, 1],
         [7, 2, 1]])
  ```
* A simple observation: when `m=1`, generating variates without replacement is trivially the same as generating with replacement.


`select`: A new `choice`-like method
------------------------------------

The proposed signature is

    def select(items, *, nsample=None, p=None, size=None, axis=None, out=None)

(Note: `axis` and `out` are not implemented in `numerand.select`, and neither is broadcasting of `items` and `p`. Also the `shuffle` parameter of `Generator.choice` is not in `select`--it wasn't needed for this trial implementation--but it would be added if necessary, depending on which efficient algorithm is eventually implemented.)

The core operation performed is *select `nsample` elements from `items` without replacement*.

*Parameters*

* `items` is the sequence of items from which to select elements.  As a convenience, `items` can also be a nonnegative integer, in which case--for the purpose of broadcasting--it behaves identical to the 1-d array `np.arange(items)`.
* `nsample` is the `m` parameter discussed above.  `select` implements a multivariate distribution, where each variate is a 1-d array of shape `(nsample,)`.   If `nsample` is None, a single element is selected (analogous to how the `size` parameter is generally handled in `numpy.random` functions and methods).
* `p`, if given, allows assigning different probablilities to each element of `items`.  It has the same meaning as in `Generator.choice`.  If `items` or `p` are 2-d or higher dimensional, the arguments broadcast, gufunc-style.  That is, for the array parameters `items` and `p`, and the scalar integer `nsample`, the gufunc shape signature would be `(n),(n)->(nsample)`.
* `size` is as discussed above in the second background note: it determines the shape of the collection of variates that are generated.  It has the same meaning as in any other multivariate distribution in `numpy.random`.
* `axis`: when the arrays `items` or `p` have more than one dimension, `axis` sets the axis along which the operation takes place.  This allows doing random selection independently along 1-d slices of `items`. *Note:* This is not the same as how `axis` is handled in `Generator.choice`. It is more consistent with, for example, `Generator.permuted` and `np.sort`.
* `out` is the usual optional output parameter.

For example,

```
In [2]: a = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

In [3]: select(a, nsample=3)  # Select 3 elements without replacement.
Out[3]: array([50, 40, 20])

In [4]: select(a, nsample=3, size=8)  # 8 repetitions of selecting 3 elements without replacement.
Out[4]: 
array([[40, 30, 50],
       [20, 30, 10],
       [40, 50, 30],
       [50, 40, 30],
       [30, 50, 20],
       [20, 50, 40],
       [20, 10, 30],
       [10, 20, 50]])

In [5]: select(a, nsample=3, p=[0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.0, 0.7], size=8)
Out[5]: 
array([[50, 30, 20],
       [50, 10, 30],
       [50, 10, 20],
       [50, 10, 30],
       [50, 10, 30],
       [50, 20, 30],
       [20, 10, 50],
       [10, 50, 30]])
```

A nice feature of this API is that, when `nsample` is `None` (which is the default), `select` naturally does random choice *with* replacement (see the third background note above). No boolean flag is necessary.  E.g.

```
In [34]: a
Out[34]: [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

In [35]: select(a)
Out[35]: np.int64(30)

In [36]: select(a, size=15)
Out[36]: array([50, 10, 20, 30, 10, 20, 10, 10, 10, 30, 40, 30, 30, 30, 50])

In [37]: select(a, p=[0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.0, 0.7], size=15)
Out[37]: array([50, 50, 50, 30, 50, 50, 30, 50, 10, 50, 50, 20, 10, 50, 50])
```

In other words, `select` can completely replace `choice`.

Looking at the implementation provided in #28306, it appears to still be very loopy: both over the the number of samples to draw and over the drawing of the samples themselves. If it helps anyone, here's a fully-vectorized implementation with an API that matches that of the existing `np.random.Generator.choice`. Moreover this is vectorized even over weights `p` that may be different for each slice of `a`. Benchmarking this on problems of various sizes / with various flags, I find that when called on unbatched data that it matches the built-in `.choice`, and when called on batched data then e.g. it is up to 40x faster (with `replace=False`, `p=...`) than looping over the built-in `.choice`, or up to 300x faster (with `replace=True`, `p=None`).

So the fast path that computes `1.0/x` when the power is -1 gives the most precise answer.  I've tested this on my machine for large samples of random integers and double precision floats, and so far `np.power(x, -1.0)` has always given an answer that is correct to machine precision.  `float_power(x, -1.0)` is occasionally less precise.

> I am really curious to know why the maximum number of dimensions in NumPy is limited to 64 only?

It's helpful in the implementation to limit it to _something_ rather than let it be unbounded. The reason for 64 is that there are only limited uses for trivial dimensions of length 1, so if we consider an array of a shape `(2, 2, 2, ..., 2)` as the minimal useful array, then this nontrivial array of 64 dimensions has 2**64 elements, which consumes the entire theoretical address space for 64-bit systems, which is the most that we currently target. There are occasionally use cases for modeling things which have many more mostly-1 dimensions, but we're happy to let those be handled outside of numpy's core data structure.

For more fun, the determinant of the transpose of that matrix is exactly zero, the LU factorization of the original matrix produces an equivalent estimate, and the QR and SVD factorizations produce determinant estimates slightly smaller than the others:
```pycon
>>> import numpy as np
>>> import numpy.linalg as la
>>> from scipy import linalg
>>> arr = np.array([[5, 5, 6], [7, 7, 5], [4, 4, 8]])
>>> la.det(arr)
-3.1974423109204565e-14
>>> la.det(arr.T)
0.0
>>> np.prod(la.svd(arr)[1])
9.990753062948142e-15
>>> np.prod(np.diag(la.qr(arr)[1]))
-9.243157666806292e-15
>>> la.slogdet(arr)
SlogdetResult(sign=-1.0, logabsdet=-31.073840089541154)
>>> np.exp(-31.07384)
3.197442597223141e-14
>>> np.prod(np.diag(linalg.lu(arr)[2]))
3.197442310920451e-14
>>> linalg.lu(arr)[0]
array([[0., 1., 0.],
       [1., 0., 0.],
       [0., 0., 1.]])
```
All of these estimates of the determinant are less than the largest element of the matrix times the size of the matrix times the resolution of the type the calculations are done in (`abs(la.det(arr)) < 1e-15 * arr.size * arr.max()`), so I would be inclined to count them as equivalent to zero.  Given the existence of the Hermite Normal Form, it is possible that the singularity threshold for an integer matrix could be *much* larger, perhaps a flat 1e-6 or even 1e-3.

[A comment on](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/27599#issuecomment-2425430019) #27599 suggests [`la.matrix_rank`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.linalg.matrix_rank.html) for determining whether a given matrix is singular; it basically combines the suggestions and rules-of-thumb above.  The actual test for singularity would then be `la.matrix_rank(arr) < min(arr.shape)`.

The behavior you’re observing is due to the inconsistent handling of NaN values between np.ma.mean and np.ma.median. 

Specifically:
` np.ma.mean` treats NaN values as if they are masked, effectively excluding them from the computation.
`np.ma.median`, on the other hand, propagates NaN values unless they are explicitly masked.


```python
import numpy as np

# Build the dummy array
arr = np.random.rand(25, 5, 5)
mask = np.zeros((25, 5, 5), dtype=bool)
mask[:, 0, 0] = True  # Mask some values
bool_arr = np.zeros((25, 5, 5), dtype=bool)
bool_arr[:, 0, 1] = True  # Introduce NaN values
arr = np.ma.MaskedArray(arr, mask=mask)
arr[bool_arr] = np.nan

# Explicitly mask NaN values
arr.mask |= np.isnan(arr)

# Compare mean and median
mean_result = np.ma.mean(arr, axis=0)
median_result = np.ma.median(arr, axis=0)

print("Mean:\n", mean_result)
print("Median:\n", median_result)
```

arr.mask |= np.isnan(arr) Ensures that all NaN values are treated as masked explicitly, which is crucial for consistent behavior.

If this goes into NumPy or SciPy, I would expect these properties:

* It is explicitly defined to be the Gram matrix (i.e. the matrix of inner products of the columns of `x`), so either `gram` or `gram_matrix` would be a reasonable name.
* It handles the complex case correctly.  Specifically, it conjugates where necessary.
* It should have the option to accept a Hermitian matrix `M` (symmetric in the real case). Also allowing it to accept the 1-d diagonal, say `w`, provides a convenient (and more efficient) way to provide `M=diag(w)`.
* It would be nice if it accepts higher dimensional inputs than what is needed for the core operation (i.e. gufunc-like, with broadcasting).

Here's a quick implementation based on `einsum`. (The indices in the first argument of `einsum` could be tweaked if different default positions of the "stacked" inputs are desired.)

```
import numpy as np


def gram(x, *, M=None, w=None):
    """
    Compute the Gram matrix.

    The Gram matrix is the matrix of inner products of the columns of `x`.
    By default, the standard Euclidean inner product <x, x> is computed.

    When `M` is provided, the inner product is <x, M@x>.  So generally `M`
    should be Hermitian (symmetric in the real case), but this is not checked
    and does not affect the calculation.

    `x` must be at least 2-d, with shape `(..., m, n)`.

    If given, 'M' must be an array with shape `(..., m, m)`.
    That is, it can be a "batch" of 2-d arrays.
    
    If given, `w` must be an array with shape `(..., m)`.
    That is, it can be a "batch" of 1-d arrays.
    Using `w` is equivalent to using `M=np.diag(w)`.

    The result has shape `(..., n, n)`.
    """
    if w is not None and M is not None:
        raise ValueError('only one of `w` or `M` may be given')
    if np.iscomplexobj(x):
        y = x.conjugate().transpose()
    else:
        y = x.transpose()
    if w is None and M is None:
        return y @ x
    if M is None:
        return np.einsum('...ik,...k,...kj->...ij', y, w, x)
    # M is not None
    return np.einsum('...ik,...kl,...lj->...ij', y, M, x)
```

There's a very strong use case for subinterpreters since PEP 684 for parallel processing that I expect would be useful to a lot of numpy client code: using subinterpreters in separate threads will enable shared memory (at least in a read-only case) with significantly less hassle than multiprocessing.

I’m also very excited about the potential opportunities of using subinterpreters with numpy, and agree with what @mdekstrand said. In particular, the latest draft of PEP 734 discusses sharing data via the buffer protocol (and already implemented in the private interpreters module since 3.13a1). Since ndarrays can export their buffer or be created from one without copies, this could be a very nice pattern:

* pickle your array with protocol 5 to get some serialized metadata plus the memoryview,
* pass that view to a bunch of interpreters (which is basically instant) as well as the small metadata,
* and unpickle: now all of them are sharing the data in each of their arrays
* And if you don’t want to worry about data races, seems like np can handle that by setting the readonly flag.

You get concurrency with performant, opt-in data sharing, without the hassles of managing subprocesses and using multiprocessing.shared_memory where you have to create a shared buffer of fixed size ahead of time and only create arrays using that. With interpreters you can take any random array you got and easily share it.

InterpreterPoolExecutor's are to be introduced in 3.14 [124548](https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/124548).

At present, numpy imports fail due to "ImportError: module numpy._core._multiarray_umath does not support loading in subinterpreters":

See following example: TPE and PPE work, IPE does not. 

```py
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
from interpreters_backport.concurrent.futures.interpreter import InterpreterPoolExecutor

def try_tpe():
    with ThreadPoolExecutor() as executor:
        executor.submit(exec, "import numpy as np;print('TPE:', np.random.rand(2))")

def try_ppe():
    with ProcessPoolExecutor() as executor:
        executor.submit(exec, "import numpy as np;print('PPE:', np.random.rand(2))")

def try_ipe():
    with InterpreterPoolExecutor() as executor:
        f = executor.submit(exec, "import numpy as np;print('IPE:', np.random.rand(2))")
        f.result()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    try_tpe()
    try_ppe()
    try_ipe()
```

There are two different problems associated with integer inputs, neither of which is restricted to unsigned integers.

(1) One problem occurs when the difference between two adjacent values cannot be represented by the integer type of the array.  This is the result of using `np.diff` in the implementation.  For example, with `x = np.array([1, -10, 126, 40], dtype=np.int8)`, the second value in `np.diff(x)` is mathematically 126 - (-10) = 136, but that value will wrap around to -120 because `np.diff` preserves the dtype and the maximum `int8` is 127.  The correct value for `np.unwrap(x, period=9)` is `[1, -1, 0, 4]`, but we actually get

```
In [156]: x
Out[156]: array([  1, -10, 126,  40], dtype=int8)

In [157]: np.unwrap(x, period=9)
Out[157]: array([ 1, -1, -4,  0], dtype=int8)
```
If we cast to an integer type with more bits, we get the correct result:
```
In [158]: np.unwrap(x.astype(np.int16), period=9)
Out[158]: array([ 1, -1,  0,  4], dtype=int16)
```

Note that the correct value is representable in the original array data type, so in theory this example could be fixed by modifying the implementation.

(2) The other problem occurs when the "correct" output cannot be represented by the input data type.  By "correct", I mean correct under the assumption that the output can represent all integers, positive or negative.  Obviously this conflicts with `np.unwrap` when the input is unsigned but the "correct" result is negative.  The problem also occurs at the large end of the unsigned type, and at the extreme ends of the signed integer types.

Examples of the second problem:

* An unsigned example
  
  ```
  In [176]: x = np.array([0, 17], dtype=np.uint8)
  
  In [177]: np.unwrap(x, period=9)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  OverflowError                             Traceback (most recent call last)
  [...]
  OverflowError: Python integer -4 out of bounds for uint8
  ```
  
  The "correct" result would be `[0, -1]`, but that result is not possible if `unwrap` preserves   the input data type.

* A signed example
  
  ```
  In [195]: x = np.array([127, 22], dtype=np.int8)
  
  In [196]: np.unwrap(x, period=9)
  Out[196]: array([ 127, -126], dtype=int8)
  ```
  
  The "correct" output would be [127, 130], but 130 ends up wrapped around to -126.

Hello @mattip,
Thank you for your reply and for outlining possible workarounds.

I have a couple of follow-up questions, mostly out of curiosity rather than a desire to push for changes:

1. You mentioned that there has been discussion about adding a `max_dims` argument to `np.array`. I think such an option would be quite useful. I'm curious if there was ever a concrete proposal (for example, a GitHub issue or NEP), and if so, why it didn't move forward.

2. Regarding `dtype=object`, I was wondering: what exactly does NumPy treat as an “object” in this context? From a Python perspective, a list is an object, but NumPy seems to treat them differently in practice. For example, when the input is a list of uniform-length lists, NumPy promotes them to arrays even when` dtype=object` is explicitly specified.

Again, thank you for your time!

`np.array()` has to do a lot of different things, inferring from context what you meant. It can't read your mind, so we have some heuristics. When you say `dtype=object` and provide it a list of lists of objects, we don't know whether you meant to create a 1D array of list objects or a 2D array of the inner objects. We apply the heuristic that when we have nested `list`s (nested `list`s being the most typical Python literal that folks use to build the objects that people provide to `np.array()`), it will go as deep as it can as long as the nesting can be interpreted as a uniform shape (i.e. all of the inner `list`s at the same level of nesting have the same length). It's a really strong signal that that's what the user wanted, even when `dtype=object`. The times when you don't, like your case, are much rarer. And we have a number of existing workarounds that folks use. I do think `max_dims` would be a good addition, but so far, folks have been happy enough with the workarounds so that no one gets up the energy to actually implement `max_dims`.

That just doesn't come up that often, and when it does, something like `awkward` is typically a better, more comprehensive solution.

That `meson` isn't added as a runtime dependency of `numpy` is on purpose, for a couple of reasons:
- `f2py` can be used for generating code without needing any build system - that is its primary purpose actually.
- `f2py -c` can work with `distutils` or `meson` or `scikit-build-core`/`cmake`, or any other build system that one may want to wire up, as documented at https://numpy.org/doc/2.3/f2py/buildtools/index.html
- `f2py -c` needs not only a build system but also compilers. That can't even be expressed in Python packaging metadata as of today.

So the expectation is that this is for the user to manage. They can install `meson` or some other build system and the compilers they want to use. 

How about we document this more clearly to close this issue? I'm thinking an info box at the top of https://numpy.org/doc/2.3/f2py/usage.html is the best place.
I also think we can probably make this error message friendlier, with a suggestion to e.g. install meson with a package manager.

In case it's helpful to anyone, here's a workaround that seems to work correctly:

```python3
import numpy as np

def argsort(a, axis=-1, descending=False):
    if descending:
        a = np.flip(a, axis)
        i = np.argsort(a, stable=True)
        i = np.flip(i, axis)
        i = a.shape[axis] - 1 - i
        return i
    else:
        return np.argsort(a, axis, stable=True)

def implies(a, b):
    return ~a | b

def main():
    a = np.array([4, 2, 2, 8, 2, 9, 1], np.uint8)
    i = argsort(a, descending=True)
    ai = a[i]
    print(i)
    print(ai)
    # The array is sorted in descending order.
    assert (ai[:-1] >= ai[1:]).all()
    # If two elements are equal, the lower-index element appears first.
    assert implies(ai[:-1] == ai[1:], i[:-1] < i[1:]).all()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

This will take quite some work here and in mypy. At a discussion held several weeks ago, the agreement was on the plan in the [README](https://github.com/numpy/numpy_stubs/blob/master/README.md). So while this will happen, adding support for checking shapes will not happen soon. There is much to decide, such as how to define syntax related to declaring array shape, and how an actual type checking implementation should work.

@shoyer: I'm not sure where this should be noted, but the framing of numpy/numpy-stubs#6 and python/typing#516 seems to indicate that you're favoring putting the full shape in the type specification: that is, for a two-dimensional array of size (M,N), the proposal seems to be that the type annotation would convey both the value of M and N.

I think we should consider a more modest version in which only the number of dimensions is tracked via the type, but not the shape itself. That is, instead of `ndarray[Shape[100, 200], Dtype]` for an array of `shape=(100,200)`, we go for `ndarray[2, Dtype]`, to indicate only the fact that the array has ndim=2.

Tracking only the rank (as opposed to the full shape) of the array through the type system is, for what it's worth, how all of the C++ tensor libraries work to the best of my knowledge. It's more consistent with the rest of the PEP484 container types as well, in the sense that the type `List[int]` doesn't track the number of elements.

@rmcgibbo Yes, this needs justification.

My reasoning for favoring specifying shapes in types comes down to:
- Rank and shape are not mutually exclusive: if we do shape, we get rank as well. We could even have an explicit `Rank` type, which we tell type checkers should be treated as equivalent to anonymous dimensions, e.g., `ndarray[Rank[2]]` could be the same as `ndarray[Shape[:, :]]`.
- For code directly using NumPy, rank checks would not be anywhere near as valuable as shape checks. The problem is that nearly NumPy operation is valid on inputs with an arbitrary number of dimensions (even between arguments, with broadcasting). Giving up on shape checks would means we couldn't type ufuncs in a useful way, or catch the common errors with broadcasting. This would basically mean reserving shape/rank checks for the (many) applications and libraries that only use on particular ranks (e.g., vectors and matrices).

With regards to C++ libraries, [Eigen](https://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/group__TutorialMatrixClass.html) at least does allow for either runtime and statically defined shapes. That said, I certainly would not bother with static/compile-time shapes on their own, because it is indeed rare that you know the exact shape of arrays before running a program. But with generics, we have the possibility of doing much more sophisticated pattern matching. This isn't feasible in C++, where you would need to use templates for every possible dimension size. In contrast, we can probably do something more sophisticated in Python to allow for typing shapes without enumerating all of them (similar to what you see in Haskell).

Shape is clearly more expressive than rank. So in that sense, I agree with both of your bulleted points above (not mutually exclusive, and static shape checks, if they worked, would provide more value to users). There are two factors on the other side that come to mind.

* In almost any real code, it will be impossible for mypy to statically infer the shapes. For example, take the following:

```
M = 5
N = 10
arr = np.zeros((M, N))
reveal_type(arr)
```

Mypy tracks the type of M and N, but not their values. It can infer the rank of `arr`, but not the full shape. Want to do something more complicated?

```
def compute_length() -> int:
    return <something>
def compute_width() > int:
    return <something>
arr = np.zeros((compute_length(), compute_width()))
reveal_type(arr)
```
Not going to work.

* If the shape is to be tracked explicitly, for example, to the best of my understanding there is no way to express even the *simplest* numpy function signatures with the current generation of PEP484/mypy. For example, take

```
# requires a type-level addition function to express the return type.
def concatenate_1d_arrays(arr1 : ndarray[D, Shape[M]], arr2 : ndarray[D, Shape[N]] -> ?
```

Take another look at [my doc on shape typing](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1vpMse4c6DrWH5rq2tQSx3qwP_m_0lyn-Ij4WHqQqRHY/edit#heading=h.rkj7d39awayl). You're right that functions like `concatenate` are hard, but I would claim that even mere matching of integer sizes (without arithmetic) along with dimension identity would be enough to be valuable:
- You could catch broadcasting errors when using ufuncs.
- You could catch errors with regards to which dimension is removed by aggregation or indexing
- You could verify that the shapes of non-concatenated axes of arrays in `concatenate` match, and are propagated to the result, e.g., `stack_matrices(x: ndarray[Shape[:, N], y: ndarray[Shape[:, N]]) -> ndarray[Shape[:, N]]`.

> In almost any real code, it will be impossible for mypy to statically infer the shapes. For example, take the following:
```
M = 5
N = 10
arr = np.zeros((M, N))
reveal_type(arr)
```

I'm not certain that mypy will be unable to infer shapes in this case. If typing adds support for literals (which is almost certainly necessary regardless for NumPy), then I imagine it will also support literals in variables, in the same way that it supports type aliases.

My suspicions are that shape tracking is (1) going to add a small marginal value, since it will be rarely be possible to statically infer them (e.g. my two examples above) in real world code, whereas it will often be possible to statically infer rank in real world code; and (2) going to add a ton of complexity. That suggests to me it's not the best place to start for the "1.0".

If there's a way to design the syntax so that it is initially rank-only, build a viable package around that, and add shape information afterwards in a second stage, then that would be my preference.

Maybe for v1.0 we could have `ndarray[2, Dtype]` be an alias for `ndarray[Shape[Any, Any], Dtype]`, ignoring the length of the shape but keeping the `ndim` in mind. This would probably be a good-ish idea to keep forward compatibility.

Edit: It might also be a good idea to have a warning if the shape contains anything other than `Any` (or similar), for now.

Realized the other day that most of what is wanted here can already be supported using `typing.Tuple` and `typing.Literal`, assuming `typing.TypeVar` behaves well with `typing.Literal` (I don't think it does with mypy). For many cases, the usual use of `@typing.overload` will be sufficient.

For example, one could type-hint `matmul` as follows:

```python
from typing import Tuple, TypeVar, overload
import numpy as np
from numpy.typing import DType, NDArray

T1 = TypeVar("T1", bound=int)
T2 = TypeVar("T2", bound=int)
T3 = TypeVar("T3", bound=int)
DTypeVar = TypeVar("DTypeVar", bound=DType)

@overload
def matmul(x1: NDArray[Tuple[T1], DTypeVar], x2: NDArray[Tuple[T1], DTypeVar], /) -> DTypeVar:
    ...

@overload
def matmul(x1: NDArray[Tuple[T1], DTypeVar], x2: NDArray[Tuple[T1, T2], DTypeVar], /) -> NDArray[Tuple[T2], DTypeVar]:
    ...

@overload
def matmul(x1: NDArray[Tuple[T1, T2], DTypeVar], x2: NDArray[Tuple[T2], DTypeVar], /) -> NDArray[Tuple[T1], DTypeVar]:
    ...

@overload
def matmul(x1: NDArray[Tuple[T1, T2], DTypeVar], x2: NDArray[Tuple[T2, T3], DTypeVar], /) -> NDArray[Tuple[T1, T3], DTypeVar]:
    ...
```

If it works with `typing.Literal`, then one would be able to track the full shape. Otherwise, only the number of dimensions can be tracked.

```python
HEIGHT = Literal[500]
WIDTH = Literal[1000]

x: NDArray[Tuple[HEIGHT, WIDTH], int] = ...
A: NDArray[Tuple[WIDTH, WIDTH], int] = ...
y: NDArray[Tuple[HEIGHT, WIDTH], int] = matmul(x, A)
```

To make it more readable, one could also alias `npt.Len = Literal` and `npt.Shape = Tuple` to be able to write like this:

```python
x: NDArray[Shape[Len[500], Len[1000]], int]
```

Although a little clunkier, it avoids the issue of type-checkers failing to recognize constants like:

```python
HEIGHT = 500
WIDTH = 1000
x: NDArray[[WIDTH, HEIGHT], DType]
```

It's also probably easier to create generics like this using `typing.Literal` to ensure it's an actual type. It also allows arbitrary lengths to be typed using `int`. Perhaps `npt.AnyLen = int` could be used as well?

```python
# dataset[index][row][col]
dataset: NDArray[Tuple[AnyLen, HEIGHT, WIDTH], DType]
```

Semantically I would also argue that it makes a lot of sense, since this is the literal type-hint for `ndarray.shape` being used here.

I've been thinking about this for a while now, and I believe that the following proposal could work. 

For the sake of brevity and readability, I'll be using the Python 3.12+ [PEP 695](https://peps.python.org/pep-0695/) syntax. Additionally, I'll prefix type parameter declarations with either a `~`, `+` or `-` to explicitly indicate their *in*-, *co*- or *contra*-variance, respectively.

## The `ndarray` shape type parameter

Currently, its type signature is `ndarray[~Shape: Any, +DType: dtype[Any]]` (the `+` indicates covariance), and has `ndarray[Shape, DType].shape: tuple[int, ...]`. 
I propose to 

1. restrict the upper bound of `Shape` to `tuple[int, ...]`
2. ~change `~Shape` to `+Shape`, i.e. make it covariant (instead of invariant)~ #26081
3. change the type of `ndarray.shape` from `tuple[int, ...]` to `Shape`

To illustrate, what is currently

```python
class ndarray[~Shape: Any, +DType: dtype[Any]]:
    shape: tuple[int, ...] 
    [...]
```

will become

```python
class ndarray[+Shape: tuple[int, ...], +DType: dtype[Any]]:
    shape: Shape
    [...]
```

(in practice `shape` will be typed as a `@property`)

This is almost always backwards compatible. The only backwards incompatible case is for annotations that bind `Shape@ndarray` to a specific type that isn't a `tuple[int, ...]`. Note that having `np.ndarray[Any, ...]` is still allowed, so that e.g. `numpy.typing.NDArray` is fully backwards-compatible.

*The upper bound of the `+Shape` type param can be made tighter, by noting the `ndim` limit of max 64, i.e. `+Shape: tuple[()] | tuple[int] | tuple[int, int] | ... # up to tuples of length 64`. However, this would become rather messy, and could negatively impact the performance of type checkers.*

## Add a shape-aware alias like `NDArray`

For the sake of backwards compatibility, `numpy.typing.NDArray` should be kept as-is. 
I propose adding a new type alias to `numpy.typing`, that has an additional variadic type parameter to indicate the shape of an array. 
Since the semantics of the `ND` prefix are now reflected through the presence of the type parameter for the shape, let's call it `Array` for now:

```python
# in numpy.typing

# equivalent to the current definition
type NDArray[+Scalar: generic] = ndarray[Any, dtype[Scalar]]

# new
type Array[*Shape: int, +Scalar: generic] = ndarray[tuple[*Shape], Scalar]
```

Unfortunately, variadic type parameters (e.g. `typing.TypeVarTuple`) cannot have an upper bound (`bound=...`). However, type checkers should be able to infer that restriction automatically, since `tuple[*Shape]` will bind to `tuple[int, ...]`, and therefore `Shape: int`.

Some examples:

```python
from typing import Literal
import numpy as np
import numpy.typing as npt

# ndarray[tuple[Literal[1]], dtype[float64]]
array_0d: npt.Array[Literal[1], np.float64] = np.array(1 / 137)

# ndarray[tuple[N], dtype[T]]
type Vector[N: int, T: np.generic] = npt.Array[N, T]

# ndarray[tuple[N, N], dtype[floating[B]]]
type Covariance[N: int, B: npt.NBitBase] = npt.Array[N, N, np.floating[B]]

# ndarray[tuple[2, 2], dtype[complexfloating[Re, Im]]
type Pauli[B: npt.NBitBase] = npt.Array[2, 2, np.complexfloating[B, B]]
```

## Updates to callable signatures

The annotations of many methods, operators, ufuncs, and other functions can now be made more specific. 

For instance, `numpy.outer(a, b, out=None)` can now be annotated as

```python
@overload
def outer[M, N, T](
    a: Array[M, Any], 
    b: Array[N, Any],
    out: Array[M, N, T] = ...,
) -> Array[M, N, T]: ...

@overload
def outer[M, N, T](
    a: Array[M, T], 
    b: Array[N, T],
    out: None = ...,
) -> Array[M, N, T]: ...

...  # overloads for the remaining dtype combinations
```

For functions with a more dynamic shape mapping, this might not be possible. For example `numpy.transpose` effectively reverses the shape of the input array. In this case, `@overload`'s could be used for the first few dimensions (e.g. 4), assuming that lower-dimensional arrays used most often.

A `MaskedArray` already supports `StringDType`. It is perfectly possible as `numpy2.3` to create a `MaskedArray` like this with missing data and all, however the issue here is that once I have it with `StringDType`, it is not possible to set a `fill_value` to this array that is actually a string.

So in the worst case scenario, this fix is just proposing consistency in the already supported datatypes (https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.dtype.kind.html).


For context, I'm an astrophysicist using regularly numpy (and other packages like astropy) to work with large data sets, that often contain string data types (for ids for stars, for example). It has always been problematic the fixed-width string data types such as `U` or `S` when comparing, modifying, joining, or cross-matching large data-sets (from a variety of sources).
`StringDType` being a variable-width data type, was a most welcome addition to address this in my opinion. Things like String truncation and unnoticed trailing spaces when creating and merging large arrays are more manageable (and forgiving) with `StringDType`, this also while keeping the capabilities of string manipulation.

As I alluded to in the PR you opened, I'd really like to see better tests for this workflow. As far as I can see in a quick check on my phone, the MaskedArray tests don't use StringDType at all and the StringDType tests don't use MaskedArray at all.

I'd rather not merge one-off fixes without broader tests, let alone any tests.

Hope that makes it clearer where I'm coming from. I'm glad you're using StringDType and you like it - you just have a use-case I didn't explicitly try to support so I bet lots of stuff is broken.

print(f"\n{np.c_[grid] =}".replace("=", "=\n"))
print(f"\n{np.c_[list(grid)] =}".replace("=", "=\n"))
print(f"\n{np.c_[tuple(grid)] =}".replace("=", "=\n"))
print(f"\n{np.c_[*grid] =}".replace("=", "=\n"))
print(f"\n{np.c_[np.array(grid)] =}".replace("=", "=\n"))
print(f"\n{np.c_[*np.array(grid)] =}".replace("=", "=\n"))
```

Encapsulating all these cases into a single, simple rule, we have:

```javascript
return x == 0 || x != x ? x : x / abs(x)
```

> I am not in favor of doing anything for object arrays,

I'd personally recommend the following approach which would handle nan, complex, fraction, float, int, you-name-it, and keep everything in its original domain for consistency:

```javascript
return x == 0 || x != x ? x : x / abs(x)  // assuming division, abs operators here return same domain as operands
```

> Encapsulating all these cases into a single, simple rule, we have:

Addendum: just realized that, since `abs(nan)` is nan and `nan/nan` is nan, my simple formula could be simplified even further to:

```

I'd personally see the specializations to specific datatypes as simply "optimized versions" of the above. So for `object` dtype, really should just fall back to the above formula for consistency with everything else, IMO.

To illustrate: 

```python

It's unclear in this particular case what d / abs(d) _should_ mean: obviously 3/abs(3) is 1, but what is `m / abs(m)`? Is that also 1, or could that actually be `m/60`, aligning more with how complex numbers work? What is the absolute value of a unit like "minute"?

IF we go with that understanding that `abs(m) == m` (rather than abs(m) == 60), then it is clear that the result of `sign` _cannot_ remain within the original domain for timedelta, because we've erased the unit via division. On the other hand, one could think of `abs(m) == 60` (where `abs(s) == 1`, basically defining a "second" to have unit-length in some "pseudo-direction").
In that case, `sign` would _preserve_ the unit. So we'd have: sign(d) == d / abs(d) == d / (3*60) == np.timedelta64(1, 's')

abs(m) == 60*abs(s)

What are the use cases of hashing that you are considering? The first "break" that you mention ("Where two values that compare equal can have different byte representations and thus different hashes") seems like correct and desirable behavior for cryptographic hashes. Those are in fact different arrays and go through code differently (e.g. complex-domain branch cuts). If I were using this hash to determine if a DAG pipeline stage should rerun or use a cached value, I do actually want to rerun that stage.

The rule you propose sounds more like the constraint on the non-crypto hash values that accelerate key-value lookups in `dict`s (where keys are compared by equality primarily and hashes just reduce the number of key-key comparisons that need to be made). But arrays typically can't be used as keys in `dict`s regardless due to a number of factors, and implementing an `np.hash()` function wouldn't enable their use in a `dict` anyways.

I'm somewhat amenable to implementing something standard in the first style of use case, but I'm also just as happy to leave this to users who know what constraints they are under and which particular set of requirements they want (maybe they _do_ want signed 0s to be treated identically).
@crusaderky can you give a little extra context for how versioned_hdf5 uses array hashes?

I'm somewhat more favorable to exposing a function that returns or yields a sequence of buffers that do our best effort at providing different unique hashable _data_ for different arrays, accounting for all the various new dtypes that do fun things with storage. Then it's up to the user to pick their own hashing algorithm (which for many purposes might be a fast non-crypto hash not in `hashlib` like [xxhash](https://xxhash.com/)).

The [`versioned_hdf5` Design docs](https://deshaw.github.io/versioned-hdf5/master/design.html), for reference.

In their use case, it seems like they have a separate content-addressable store of array chunks for each HDF5 dataset (i.e. mapping a SHA256 hash of the chunk data to the actual stored chunk data). Each hashable chunk just needs to be compared against other chunks from the same large array, therefore the same dtype. For their purposes, I think the fact that the hash of `np.zeros(10, dtype=np.uint64)` equaling the hash of `np.zeros(10, dtype=np.float64)`, for example, is not a problem. I don't think `np.array(["ab", "cd"])` and `np.array(["abcd"])` would be either because you wouldn't actually have to deal with `<U2` and `<U4` arrays.

What people actually want from a hashing scheme is really dependent on these details, so I'm not much in favor of spending much effort making a one-size-fits all, official numpy hash. That said, it might be worth thinking about how to expose hashable buffers better for the newer dtypes with fancier storage.

This is also related to recent work in Zarr to add support for arbitrary data types (https://github.com/zarr-developers/zarr-python/pull/2874) - it'd be neat if this API could be used over there as well.

The general `arr.__reduce_ex__(pickle.HIGHEST_PROTOCOL)` is almost there if it would use `PickleBuffer` more, but in the case of `StringDType`, it's returning a list of strings for its data (which is workable, but takes some more effort).

But for the `versioned_hdf5` case, a numpy-generic implementation may not be fit for purpose. The main thing they need to figure out is if there is an existing HDF5-serialized chunk that's usable to represent the incoming chunk. Since HDF5 has its own rules, particularly for strings, I'm not sure that a numpy-generic implementation would be usable. Even if we came up with a good rule for `StringDType` or `dtype=object` for general purposes, it's quite possible that it won't match the semantics needed for `versioned_hdf5`. For example, we might (validly) hash a pickle of these arrays, but that could well result in different hashes for what would end up being the same HDF5 chunk.

> [@crusaderky](https://github.com/crusaderky) can you give a little extra context for how versioned_hdf5 uses array hashes?

versioned-hdf5 hashes each chunk of a dataset. When two chunks have the same hash, you end up with only one hash on disk. This deduplicates the use cases where

1. one writes two identical chunks in different positions,
2. one updates a chunk to have the exact same data as it had in the previous version,
3. one updates a chunk to have the same data the same or another chunk had at some point in any previous version, not necessarily the one immediately before.

This deduplication exclusively happens within the same dataset, and you can't change dtype across versions. So even if `np.array(["ab", "cd"])` and `np.array(["abcd"])` have the same hash it's not a problem (h5py doesn't have `U2` and `U4`; those two are stored as `S2` and `S4`).

A big caveat however is StringDType vs. object strings. Because there is no difference between the two in HDF5, it was decided in h5py not to store any metadata to tell them apart. You can store StringDType chunks and read them back as object strings (possibly with numpy 1.x). Documentation here: https://docs.h5py.org/en/3.14.0/strings.html#numpy-variable-width-strings

As a direct consequence of versioned-hdf5 mirroring the design of h5py, **StringDType and object-type strings must return the same hash.**

The current algorithm for both is straightforward: for every point, 
1. encode the string to bytes as utf-8
2. digest the length of the bytes as uint64 little-endian
3. digest the bytes (no zero termination)

https://github.com/deshaw/versioned-hdf5/blob/34bbe8be50b31efa65cd4b4b17cfb1bd466915be/versioned_hdf5/hashtable.py#L127-L139
The code linked above does not handle StringDType yet, but it will need to follow the same algorithm.
(Yes the above snippet is excruciatingly slow to run because it's all pure python, but that's a separate issue 🙄 )

If numpy were to introduce hashing support for StringDType, us versioned-hdf5 maintainers would be willing to consider a one-off breakage in our hashing algorithm (we have an algorithm versioning and auto-migration system to cope with events like this). However, we would still need to retain hashing parity between StringDType and object strings, and would need to retain support with NumPy 1.x for a long time too, so converting object strings to StringDType before hashing is not an option on the table.

> For example, we might (validly) hash a pickle of these arrays, but that could well result in different hashes for what would end up being the same HDF5 chunk.

At the moment it is possible, and not terribly complicated, to rewrite versioned-hdf5 in any other language for which there is already an HDF5 library (which may or may not be a wrapper around libhdf5 C). The alternative implementations would need to match the hashes we are generating in the Python implementation.
There aren't any alternative versioned-hdf5 libraries _today_, but we're uneager to preclude that opportunity, so hashing the pickle is not a good idea for us.

I have performance concerns re. the whole idea of "hashable buffers".

It's both straightforward and performant to write a C iteration that does exactly the same of what we're doing in versioned-hdf5:
1. iterate on the flattened array
2. for every point, call NpyString_load
3. calculate uint64 little endian size from `size_t npy_static_string.size` (a no-op on x86_64 and arm64/aarch64)
4. update the hash with the above
5. update the hash with `npy_static_string->buf`

For non-contiguous arrays this is even faster than calling `hashlib.hash.update(array)`, because no contiguous temporary copy needs to be generated.

So I think what we're looking for is a new C API in CPython that allows you to iterate across all buffers of an object, which then `hashlib` can start using if available. This new API could yield buffers much more granular than what is exposed today as pickle 5 buffers.

In other words:
- expand the current buffer API to be able to return multiple buffers
- add a flag that informs the buffer producer if we're going to wrap each individual buffer in a python object or if it's a fast C iteration; e.g. numpy for StringDType would yield individual strings only in the latter case. 

I wonder however if `ndarray.__reduce_ex__(5)` would actually be slower if it returned a `pickle.PickleBuffer` object for each point instead of the `list[str]` that returns today? I guess maybe not, but then there would be a bottleneck in the `buffer_callback` of `pickle.dump`?

Given your constraints, I think you're probably better off just testing for `StringDType` explicitly and iterating over values one by one like you do with `dtype=object`. I suspect that all of the opportunities to more efficiently pull out hashable `StringDType` buffers would make the hash different from how you need to do `dtype=object`. The most correct way to produce the hash for these two cases would probably be to see if you can construct the HDF5 chunk somehow (or at least the in-memory C representation that the HDF5 C API is expecting) and hash that, but I don't know if the `h5py` Cython API that you have available to you supports that (`str2vlen()`?).
No, the conversion to hdf5 contiguous internal representation is way too low in the call stack (and further in time too) to be able to tap into it.

I was thinking more of "do it twice"; i.e. do the conversion just to compute the hash then throw it away. It's quite likely faster than your current pure Python iteration. Given your constraints, you will basically have to replicate the logic of that implementation in detail in any case.

> I'm somewhat more favorable to exposing a function that returns or yields a sequence of buffers that do our best effort at providing different unique hashable data for different arrays, accounting for all the various new dtypes that do fun things with storage.

We would likely need to support multiple data buffers for complex cases like `StringDType`. It could be nice for interoperability as well, if it can stay forward-compatible and still minimal. The binary format should keep things efficient, though managing the layout could get tricky.

I am only able to reach slightly faster performance than PCG64 because the API is so slow. Asking for 64 bits at a time - releasing GIL and all that for it - is a problem. Much more time is spent on function calls than on actual generation. If the bit generation API is ever going to be developed, I would suggest ditching the different data types produced and instead letting a bit generator simply fill a buffer of bytes (of large size when a large amount of randomness is requested).

Ideally a buffer would be supplied by caller, avoiding memcpy for large amounts of data.

Having to produce uint32 and double as well in bit generator seems odd. Distributions should take care of that instead.

Granted, some generators that use modulo other than 2**8n have a disadvantage with a byte-based API. But then, I would argue all the legacy generators can be replaced with ChaCha which has higher performance and better random numbers.

> I am only able to reach slightly faster performance than PCG64 because the API is so slow.

[SFC64 reaches noticeably (but not stunningly) faster performance than PCG64](https://numpy.org/doc/1.26/reference/random/performance.html), even with the same API overheads.

> Asking for 64 bits at a time - releasing GIL and all that for it - is a problem.

I'm not sure what you mean. We generally [release the GIL once](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/main/numpy/random/_bounded_integers.pyx.in#L365-L366) and call the `next_uint64` and other `bitgen_t` functions many times when we fill large arrays.

> If the bit generation API is ever going to be developed, I would suggest ditching the different data types produced and instead letting a bit generator simply fill a buffer of bytes (of large size when a large amount of randomness is requested).

The problem is that filling a buffer with bytes is a very rare use case for `np.random`. That's not a case we care to optimize for. While there are some bulk operations that could be written in the form of "fill any array of bulk bytes, then do operations on that array", most of the interesting things in the `Generator` API can't be written that way (or would be too awkward to code that way for the performance gain we would get out of it). The C function pointer call overhead of each `next_uint64` is not insignificant, but in most codepaths is one of quite a few function calls already.

> Having to produce uint32 and double as well in bit generator seems odd. Distributions should take care of that instead.

Different PRNGs have different native outputs. `MT19937` outputs `uint32` words while `PCG64` and the other newer `BitGenerator`s natively output `uint64`. While most implementations should reuse [the common utility function](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/main/numpy/random/_common.pxd#L68-L69) for converting `uint64` draws to `double`s, there are a handful of PRNGs out there that natively output float-point numbers or a prime-sized integer range. Because each of these 3 functions are easy enough to implement from the whichever is native (and also because new `BitGenerator`s are rare), we did decide to have `BitGenerator`s implement all 3 in whatever way is the most well-adapted to the algorithm's native output. If it were harder to do or the task more common, we might have chosen otherwise.

> [SFC64 reaches noticeably (but not stunningly) faster performance than PCG64](https://numpy.org/doc/1.26/reference/random/performance.html), even with the same API overheads.

A quick set of benchmarks, using `bitgen.random_raw(size=134217728)` to generate 1 GiB of randomness. A no-op of `return 4;` takes 230ms, SFC64 takes 290ms, PCG64 450ms and my implementation 435ms. As opposed to 135ms generating into a Python buffer without Numpy.Random, avoiding internal buffer & memcpy too.

For perspective, `Generator(any of them).normal(size=134217728)` takes 1.1 seconds.

I guess the overhead is quite reasonable for this usage, and SFC64 indeed is extremely fast.

`BitGenerator.__init__()` (re)sets the state to a null pointer before trying to process the arguments. When you instantiate the object and then (re)run the `__init__()` with an invalid argument, the state gets (re)set but the exception gets in the way. In typical usage, this exception won't be a problem because one typically instantiates and runs the `__init__()` in the same expression before the user gets a hold of the instance, so they never get a chance to call methods on the invalid instance. But in this circumstance of rerunning `__init__()`, you already have a reference to the instance.

https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/main/numpy/random/bit_generator.pyx#L525

Another, slightly more realistic, reproducer would be to call `__new__()` then `__init__()` separately.

```python
>>> import numpy as np
>>> bg = np.random.PCG64.__new__(np.random.PCG64)
>>> bg.random_raw()
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
AttributeError                            Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[3], line 1
----> 1 bg.random_raw()
File bit_generator.pyx:663, in numpy.random.bit_generator.BitGenerator.random_raw()
File _common.pyx:95, in numpy.random._common.random_raw()
AttributeError: __exit__
>>> bg.lock is None
True
>>> bg.__init__(("",))
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ValueError                                Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[7], line 1
----> 1 bg.__init__(("",))
File _pcg64.pyx:123, in numpy.random._pcg64.PCG64.__init__()
File bit_generator.pyx:535, in numpy.random.bit_generator.BitGenerator.__init__()
File bit_generator.pyx:315, in numpy.random.bit_generator.SeedSequence.__init__()
File bit_generator.pyx:389, in numpy.random.bit_generator.SeedSequence.get_assembled_entropy()
File bit_generator.pyx:148, in numpy.random.bit_generator._coerce_to_uint32_array()
File bit_generator.pyx:138, in numpy.random.bit_generator._coerce_to_uint32_array()
ValueError: unrecognized seed string
>>> bg.lock is None
False
>>> bg.random_raw()
[1]    2766765 segmentation fault (core dumped)  ipython --profile doctest
```

From the first example, we can see that we can prevent _most_ of the badness if we also make sure to reset the `lock` attribute back to `None` if the rest of the `__init__()` fails (e.g. with a `try: except Exception: self.lock = None; raise`. Access to the state should be protected by the lock everywhere, so keeping it `None` when we think it is likely to be invalid will cause graceful(ish) exceptions instead of segmentation faults. This probably only needs to be done in `BitGenerator.__init__()`, but `Philox.__init__()` might also need a similar treatment in case its handling of its `key` argument fails.

@asmeurer pointed out to me that we should add a proper scalar type. Right now stringdtype's scalar is `str`, which doesn't inherit from `np.generic`, so stringdtype ends up as an oddball in the API from the perspective of the type hierarchy of the scalar types.

We can fix this by defining a proper scalar type that wraps a single packed string entry and exposes an API that is duck-compatible with `str`, making use of the ufunc implementations we're adding.

This may also lead to performance improvements, since scalar indexing won't need to copy to python's internal string representation.

I don't think this needs to happen for 2.0 since this is something we can improve later and I doubt it will have major user-facing impacts, since object string arrays also effectively have a `str` scalar.

Supporting structured dtypes is possible in principle but we punted on it for the initial version because it would add a bunch of complexity. The structured dtype code inside numpy (let alone in external libraries) makes strong assumptions about dtype instances being interchangeable, which aren't valid for stringdtype.

One path forward would be adding a mode to stringdtype that always heap-allocates. This isn't great for performance or cache locality, but does mean that the packed strings always store heap pointers and the dtype instance does not store any sidecar data. I'm not sure how hard that would be - the structured dtype code is quite complicated and I'm not sure how easy it is to determine whether a stringdtype value lives inside a structured dtype vs a stand-alone stringdtype instance.

Another thing I have in mind is to eventually add a fixed-width string mode to stringdtype, which would we could also straightforwardly support in structured dtypes, although if you need variable-width strings that doesn't help much.

Oh and quick typing tip;

patterns like this one

```
@overload
def equal(x1: U_co, x2: U_co) -> NDArray[np.bool]: ...
@overload
def equal(x1: B_co, x2: B_co) -> NDArray[np.bool]: ...
@overload
def equal(x1: S_co, x2: S_co) -> NDArray[np.bool]: ...
```

can be rewritten as

```
_T_UBS = TypeVar("_T_UBS", U_co, B_co, S_co)

def equal(x1: _T_UBS, x2: _T_UBS) -> NDArray[np.bool]: ...
```

Just keep in mind this is one of the few cases where such a "type parameter with constraints" should actually be used, i.e. to "compress" overloads. I could explain the gory details of this if you're interested, but this probably isn't the best place for that 😛

class ndarray[ShapeT: tuple[int, ...], DTypeT: dtype]:
    # --snip--

	@overload
    def __radd__[T](self, lhs: CanAdd[Self, T], /) -> T: ...
    # --insert remaining overloads--
```

That overload should be above the ones that match against the array-likes & co. The idea is to first attempt to "return to sender", as this will effectively "call"  the `__add__` of the left-hand-side. SO `self.__rhs__(x)` will return `x.__add__(self)` (assuming that the type of `x` implements `__add__`). And since `pd.Series.__add__` is a thing, this *should* work. Even if `lhs` is `np.ndarray`, it should return the same type as it does right now :)

However, mypy will only understand this if `lhs.__add__` is **not** overloaded. That's because mypy's constraint solver does not implement *constraint sets*. Pyright has *some* support for that, but if there are multiple overloads that match, then it will *union* their result types, instead of returning the first one, which does not conform to the typing spec (maybe you see the irony). This behavior is by design.  `unwrap` looks at the *differences* from one value to the next.  Whether or not a value is changed depends only on its difference from the previous value. It does not change the first value.

I'm closing the issue, but anyone can continue the discussion of this behavior.  If there is enough interest, we could convert this to an enhancement request to provide an option for `unwrap` to move the first point to the fundamental domain and then unwrap from there.

1.  **Original Code Behavior:** The numpy.where(condition, x, y) function, as used in your example np.where(a > 2, 0, 2), correctly produces array([2, 2, 0, 0]). This is not a bug but the intended element-wise selection behavior of np.where when x and y are provided.
2. **Intended Use of np.where:**  When x and y are given, np.where returns an array of the same size as the condition, with elements chosen from x or y based on the condition.
3. **The "Correction" (for Filtering):**  f your goal was to filter the original array a to only include values greater than 2 (i.e., [3, 4]), the correct and most Pythonic NumPy way to achieve this is by using  _ _boolean indexing__:
     filtered_array = a[a > 2]

The case of `x` or `y` being scalars is also addressed in the last docstring example - this is the result of broadcasting, which is a fundamental numpy feature.

Personally, I think that `issubdtype` is behaving as it should, here.

In general, you should not pass a value `x: T` to a function if `T` is not in the domain of that function.

in this case, the domain of `issubdtype` is identical to that of the `numpy.dtype` constructor.So if `dtype(x)` is not allowed, then `issubdtype` also should not be allowed. 

The name also is pretty clear about this, as it reads "is sub-dtype". I can only interpret that to mean "is the dtype(-like) `arg1` a subtype of the dtype(-like) `arg2`?". So in that sense, the premise of his function is that both inputs must be dtype-likes. If not, then you've passed in invalid type, and raising a `TypeError` is IMO the most appropriate response.

Also, why not just place the `issubdtype` call within a `try:` block if you're unsure about whether the input is actually dtype-like? IMHO that would be the idiomatic approach here.

You are falling afoul of broadcasting. An array of shape [6000, 6000, 6000] is returned from combining [6000, 6000] and [6000, 6000, 1].  This large allocation might be exceeding the memory in your system. NumPy cannot predict that the system will run out of memory, it can only try and fail.

@iceback if your error was similar to what I had, which was `No module named 'numpy.core._multiarray_umath'`, this is caused by not installing numpy with the correct OS.

AWS lambda is going to run AWS linux at runtime, so any target-installed packages should be installed with the proper OS. If you target install `numpy` to a `package` directory via ` pip install --target ./package numpy`, and you are running another OS (such as macOS), then this will fail because the target installation assumes that the OS will not change from your native OS.

To get around this, you have two options:

1. Perform the target installation from a machine running AWS Linux, such as an EC2 instance. This worked great for me.
2. Figure out how to specify the runtime OS in your target install command. If you find a good way to do this, please share 😄

@iceback  Ya this was frustrating when I first did it, but it is definitely possible. I currently run Lambda functions with Python 3.7 with the 3 packages you mentioned. 

How I performed step 1. above involved following the steps outlined in **Updating a Function with Additional Dependencies**, described [here](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-python-how-to-create-deployment-package.html). For simplicity sake, I am going to assume that your local python file is named _pony.py_ and the lambda_function is invoked with the _ride_pony_ function. 

1. **Launch** and **connect** to an EC2 instance, such as an EC2 micro instance. Find instructions [here](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/EC2_GetStarted.html). Ensure that the instance runs AWS Linux.  
2. Check that python3 is installed. If it is not installed, install it with `sudo yum install python3 -y`
3. Make a directory for your local packages. `mkdir package`
4. Install the libraries you want to use in Lambda. FYI I always call pip as a module to avoid confusion between Python2 and Python3 pips. Also, some installation-order may be preferred in these installations and that may be worth researching. 
- `python3 -m pip install --target ./package numpy`
- `python3 -m pip install --target ./package pandas`
- `python3 -m pip install --target ./package scipy`
5. Move into installation directory with `cd package`
6. Zip the installation directory with `zip -r9 ../pony.zip .`
7. Now, from your **local** machine, scp _pony.zip_ from your EC2 instance to your local with the directions [here](https://github.com/juanfrans/notes/wiki/Copying-Files-Between-Local-Computer-and-Instance-(AWS)).
8. From your **local**,  zip _pony.py_ into _pony.zip_. `zip -g pony.zip pony.py`. Your zip file now contains **your** lambda code along with the python modules needed, which were installed to target with an AWS Linux OS. 
9. Upload the zip file to S3 (which allows for larger lambda functions, up to 50 MB). If your code is small, you can skip to step 10. 
10. Go into your lambda function (or update from the CLI) to use the code in pony.zip for that lambda function

**Ensure that your lambda function points to & executes your filename and main function,  _pony.ride_pony_, if it is not the default _lambda_function.lambda_handler_

Thanks for the code that demonstrates the issue.

The problem is that in `hist1d.__init__()`, `self.hist` is initialized like this:

```
        self.hist,edges = np.histogram([], bins=self.bins)
```

The `weights` parameter is not given, so `self.hist` will be an array of *integers*.

Then in the `fill()` method, you update `self.hist` like this:

```
        hist,edges = np.histogram(arr, bins=self.bins, weights = [weight]*len(arr))
        self.hist += hist
```

where the default value for `weight` is 1.0. That means that `hist` will be an array with data type `float64`.  The problem occurs in `self.hist += hist`.  `self.hist` has integer type, but `hist` has `float64` type, so that in-place update is not allowed.

There are at least two ways you can handle this.

*   Initialize `self.hist` to have `float64` type by passing in a `weights` array with dtype `float64` that has length 0, or by casting the result of `np.histogram()` to `float64` before assigning it to `self.hist`. E.g. this would do it:

    ```
            self.hist,edges = np.histogram([], bins=self.bins, weights=np.array([], dtype=np.float64))
    ```
    The default dtype of `np.array([])` is `float64`, so that use of `dtype=np.float64` isn't necessary, but given the context of this question, it seems useful to include it. (Explicit is better than implicit and all that.)

    Even simpler would be to initialize `self.hist` with an array of zeros of the appropriate length instead of calling `np.histogram()` to create it, but you might like the consistency of using `np.histogram()` with an empty data set.

*or*

*   Replace the in-place update of `self.hist` with regular addition, e.g.

    ```
            self.hist = self.hist + hist
    ```
    NumPy will not complain about adding integer and float arrays. That code will create a new float array and assign it to `self.hist`.

Your method for counting the number of business days in a month (i.e. pass in the first and last days of the month to `busday_count`) is not correct.  When the last day of the month is not a business day, you get the actual number of business days, but when the last day of the month is a business day, you get one less than the actual number of business days.

Instead, you should pass in the first day of the month for the begin date, and the first day of the following month as the end date. E.g.

```

Thanks for reporting.  The difference is actually that the `repr` for datetime64 NaT doesn't include the unit (while it does for `timedelta64`, which I agree is better):
```python
np.datetime64("nat", "ms")
# np.datetime64('NaT')
np.datetime64("nat", "ms").dtype
# dtype('<M8[ms]')
np.datetime64("nat").astype(np.dtype("datetime64[ns]")).dtype
# dtype('<M8[ns]')
```
So, the unit is correctly preserved/stored, but not correctly shown.

The (ancient) reason is presumably, that `datetime` prints dates as e.g. `"2014-12-12T12:12:12"` which _usually_ implicitly indicates the unit by how much is printed (e.g. in that case it stops with seconds).

I would agree we should show it for `NaT` and honestly wouldn't showing it generally (although we should maybe discuss it and/or include that in the `print_options` `legacy` option).

So, careful, we don’t want to wholesale replace API usages. Sometimes we intentionally create borrowed references. 

Any usages where in the same region of code we first create a borrowed reference and then soon after upgrade it to an owned reference by calling `Py_INCREF` can be replaced by `GetItemRef`. Replacing those usages (and deleting the subsequent `INCREF`) shouldn’t introduce new reference cou ting bugs unless we’re only doing an `INCREF` conditionally.

Basically, be careful, because reference counting bugs can be hard to track down and spot, and we don’t want to introduce any new ones in a refactor.

I believe that all cases of unannotated code that were valid with `numpy<2.2` but invalid with `>=2.2` (such as #27957), are limited to mypy, and do not occur with `(based)?pyright`.

There are two distinct `numpy==2.2.0` changes that could cause this. One is related to the ongoing work to support shape-typing, and the other has to do with changes made to `float64` and `complex128`. Both these cases are only an issue for mypy users. But all that's needed to fix this, is to help mypy a bit by add a single type annotation.

## shape-typing

The shape-typing mypy issues are all caused by https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/27211, which changed the shape-type "default" of `ndarray` from `Any` to `tuple[int, ...]`. Without this change, shape-typing simply wouldn't be possible to achieve practice (which has to do with the undefined behavior of `@overload` in the presence of `Any`).

With `numpy>=2.2.0`, the following (valid) code will cause mypy (and only mypy) to report an error:

```py
import numpy as np

x = np.arange(2)
x = x + 1
```

```
Incompatible types in assignment (expression has type "ndarray[tuple[int, ...], dtype[signedinteger[Any]]]", variable has type "ndarray[tuple[int], dtype[signedinteger[Any]]]")
```

Since numpy 2.2.0, the return type of `np.arange(2)` is an `ndarray` with a 1-dimensional shape-type, i.e. `ndarray[tuple[int], dtype[signedinteger]]`.
But `x + 1` does not (yet) take the shape-types of the input into account, and in this case returns `NDArray[signedinteger]`, which resolves to `ndarray[tuple[int, ...], dtype[signedinteger]]`.
It's not allowed to assign `tuple[int, ...]` to `tuple[int]`, so it also isn't allowed to assign `ndarray[tuple[int, ...], _]` to a `ndarray[tuple[int], _]`.

And Mypy *only* looks at `x = np.arange(2)` when it infers the type of `x`, so it immediately determines that `x: ndarray[tuple[int], dtype[signedinteger]]`, even if this is contradicted on the very next line.

So to work around this, we need to help mypy a bit by explicitly annotating `x`:

```py
import numpy as np
import numpy.typing as npt

x: npt.NDArray[np.integer] = np.arange(2)
x = x + 1
```

## `float64` and `complex128`

Before `2.2.0`, `float64` and `complex128` were incorrectly annotated type-aliases of `floating[_64Bit]` and `complexfloating[_64Bit, _64Bit]`, respectively. These changes were made in https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/27334, and apply to `complex128` in the same way as `float64`. So for the sake of brevity, I'll limit this to `float64`.

This change fixes two large issues:

1. At runtime, `float64` subclasses `floating`, but the stubs incorrectly annotated `float64` as a (restricted) *alias* of `floating`. The result is that `x: float64 = floating[Any]` will now be rejected, as it should (because it's type-unsafe).
2. `float64` is *also* a subclass of `builtins.float`, but the stubs did not reflect this. This was causing e.g. `x: float = np.float64(42)` to be falsely rejected on `numpy<2.2.0`, even though it's perfectly type-safe.



So for example, mypy (and only mypy) will reject the last of the following example

```py
y = np.array([], np.float64)
y = y + 1 
```

```
Incompatible types in assignment (expression has type "ndarray[tuple[int, ...], dtype[floating[Any]]]", variable has type "ndarray[tuple[int, ...], dtype[float64]]")
```

The `np.array([], np.float64)` expression evaluates to a `NDArray[float64]` type. But adding `1` to this, results in a `NDArray[floating]` type. But since `numpy>=2.2.0` it's no longer the case that `floating` is assignable to `float64` (because that'd be type-unsafe), so we also can't assign `NDArray[floating]` to `NDArray[float64]`.

This causes mypy to (falsely) reject `y = y + 1`, just like it rejected `x + 1` in the shape-typing example. We can also work around this in the same way:

```py
y: npt.NDArray[np.floating] = np.array([], dtype=np.float64)
y = y + 1
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Note that mypy will (still) accept the following:
> 
> ```py
> y4 = np.array([], dtype=np.float32)
> reveal_type(y4 + 1)  # ndarray[tuple[int, ...], dtype[floating[Any]]]
> y4 = y4 + 1
> ```
> 
> We see here that `y4 + 1` is inferred as `ndarray[tuple[int, ...], dtype[floating[Any]]]`, which is identical to the type of `y + 1`.
> So the errors that mypy reports are not caused by regressions or bugs; they are the consequence of a necessary improvement. And this is why these reported mypy errors are, in fact, *falsy positives*.

This is what I mean with "type-unsafe":

```py
import numpy as np
from typing import NewType

# library

Size = NewType("Size", int)
type SquareMatrix[N: Size, T: np.number] = np.ndarray[tuple[N, N], np.dtype[T]]

def list_matmul[N: Size, T: np.number](matrices: SquareMatrix[N, T], /) -> SquareMatrix[N, T]:
    out = matrices[0].copy()
    for matrix in matrices[1:]:
        out @= matrix
    return out

...

# user code

pauli = [
    np.array([[0,   1], [1,  0]], np.complex128),
    np.array([[0, -1j], [1j, 0]], np.complex128),
    np.array([[1,   0], [0, -1]], np.complex128),
]
list_matmul(pauli)  # accepted, and returns `np.eye(2) * 1j`

pauli.extend(pauli[1])  # woops, forgot the `:`  <-- type checker error
list_matmul(pauli)  # raises a `ValueError`
```

Maybe it's not the best example, but the outcome is the same if you append a non-square matrix, e.g. of shape `(1, 2)`. Type-checkers are meant to prevent such mistakes, and NumPy 2.2 makes it easier for them to do so.

In the NumPy 2.2.0 release we made `np.float64` an actual subclass both `np.floating` and `float` (the `builtins` one). Before 2.2.0, it was simply an alias of `np.floating`, which was incorrect for several reasons, which I outlined in #27334.

One of the consequences of this incorrect definition on `numpy<2.2`, is that type-checkers allowed you to assign `x: np.floating` to `y: np.float64`. But since `float64` is a subclass of `floating` (at runtime), that shouldn't be allowed, because it is *type-unsafe*. To see why, consider this example:

```py
import numpy as np

x: np.floating = np.float32()
y: np.float64 = x
```

So you're effectively assigning a `float32` to `float64` here, which is clearly type-unsafe. Before NumPy 2.2, this was just as invalid as it is now. But because `float64` was incorrectly defined, type checkers could see that this was, in fact, an error. 

I understand that it can be frustrating to have to change a lot of your annotations. But it's not because of a regression that you have to do that. It's because your annotations were type-unsafe, and NumPy 2.2 made it possible for type-checkers to help you fix it.
